A cosmetic-but-misleading console note in the shared `sv` `--design-dir` resolver. items.title: fix: authentication, facility-charge detection, and honest read quality
items.body:
The three open caveats, closed or made explicit.

## 1. Authentication — this was the serious one

`user_id` arrived as a form field. Any caller could read or write any patient's bills by changing a number, on **protected health information**.

Registration now issues a bearer token, stored only as a SHA-256 digest. Upload, appeal and dashboard require it, and the owner comes from the token — a `user_id` in the form is ignored.

**Two further holes closed with it**, both worse than the first:
- `/api/appeal/<id>` fetched a bill by id alone — any authenticated caller could read every patient's bills
- `/api/dashboard/<user_id>` trusted the id in the path

Verified:

```
no token            -> 401 Authentication required.
bad token           -> 401 That token is not valid.
cross-user appeal   -> 404 Bill not found
cross-user dashboard-> 403 Not your dashboard.
own appeal          -> 200
```

Deliberately small — no passwords, no expiry, no rotation. It closes the hole it exists to close and `auth.py` says so plainly.

## 2. Facility charges are now named, not silently refused

A revenue code marks a line as the hospital billing for its own room, equipment and staff — paid under **OPPS** (outpatient) or **DRGs** (inpatient), not the physician fee schedule. Those lines now report:

> Facility charge (revenue code 0450). Hospital facility charges are paid under OPPS or DRGs, not the physician fee schedule — comparing this line to PFS would be the wrong benchmark, not a close one.

This makes something uncomfortable visible: **an itemized hospital statement is almost entirely facility charges**, so PFS prices none of it. That was already true. The difference is the product now says so instead of quietly returning nothing.

Professional-services bills (office visits, therapy, imaging reads) still price fully — 6 of 7 lines on the sample.

## 3. Read quality — a bad scan no longer looks like a clean bill

Finding no codes was indistinguishable from finding no problems. Responses now carry `read_quality`:

| status | meaning |
|---|---|
| `failed` | OCR errored |
| `poor` | almost no text — scan too low-contrast or skewed |
| `no_codes` | text read, nothing matched — likely a summary bill, ask for itemized |
| `ok` | good read |

The UI surfaces all three, and registers/stores a token automatically so the demo still opens and works.

items.title: feat(engine): pre-LLM dedup — skip extraction for verbatim restatements
items.body:
First item from the development plan (W1, P0 — cut write cost). Cuts the write path to **0 LLM calls** when a message restates facts that are already current.

## How it works
Before calling the extractor, `add()` checks whether the exact utterance (case/whitespace-normalized) previously produced fact(s) that are **all still active**. If so, re-extraction would only `DEDUP` them (the existing RESTATEMENT branch in `_apply`), so the call is skipped and `DEDUP` is returned directly.

## Why it can't cause a staleness regression
The skip fires **only** when every statement from that utterance is currently `ACTIVE`. If any has been superseded/retracted/flagged/pending — the slot changed since — it falls through to the extractor, so a restatement that should now supersede is never skipped. It never uses fuzzy similarity, so `"5 mg"` vs `"7 mg"` can't be conflated.

## Config
On by default. `VAYL_DEDUP_PREFILTER=off` restores always-extract.

## Tests (offline, deterministic)
`tests/test_dedup_prefilter.py` spies the extractor and asserts: skip on unchanged restatement (0 extra calls), whitespace/case normalization, **fall-through after the value changes** (supersede back), no skip for a new fact, and the disable flag. Full suite stays green; ruff clean.

Note: I can't run the keyed `eval_reconcile` silently-wrong benchmark here — recommend one run on `gpt-5-mini` to confirm the rate is unchanged before relying on it in production (though the skip is a provable no-op by construction).

items.title: milestone 101: the L4 comparison, measured instead of assumed
items.body:
The block said the published L4 comparison converted the wrong benchmark. It did, and the lane found **three** independent errors in that paragraph rather than one, pointing in different directions:

1. **Wrong plane** — kernel-side `ipc_rtt` converted where seL4's numbers are user-to-user. Inflates our disadvantage.
2. **Wrong build** — the ~705 ns figure it converted was a **debug** number from 2026-07-23. Deflates it, by more than the plane costs.
3. **Wrong convention**, which nobody had flagged: seL4 publishes **one-way** costs (413 cycles call, 426 reply), and ours is a round trip, so the old comparison doubled the ratio for free.

Errors 1 and 3 inflate, 2 deflates, so "4 to 7 times heavier" landed somewhere plausible **by cancellation**.

**The machine also contradicted this milestone's own arithmetic, and the lane said so rather than delivering the predicted number.** The block forecast 12-24x by converting the *debug* EL0 figure, repeating error 2 and keeping error 3. On a clean release run the corrected ratio is **~1.1x to 1.7x**. The note's assumed 3.2 GHz was also not this machine (an M3 at 4.05 GHz P-core).

Measured on five boots off one build, both figures from every boot, host load recorded rather than claimed silent: `ipc_rtt` 46 ns median, `ipc_rtt_el0` **350 ns**, `null_syscall` 27 ns. Agrees with the 2026-07-29 refresh within noise, so nothing had regressed; only the paragraph was wrong.

The caveats section is now deliberately longer than the number, **because the correction makes us look better and that is exactly when honesty is cheapest to skip**: 2015 versus 2023 silicon, their fastpath on and ours absent, their two syscalls against our four, and a clock assumed because HVF exposes no PMU. The 705-versus-951 discrepancy turns out not to be a contradiction but two debug singles published without their build profile; every figure now carries one.

No benchmark code was touched. Three roadmap rows quote the retracted arithmetic and need integrator fixes at merge, including milestone 74, which held a stale block quote of it for twelve days with no gate able to see it.

items.title: feat: price bills against the real CMS fee schedule
items.body:
## Summary

Replaces `MOCK_CPT_DB` — ten rates someone typed — with the **CMS Physician Fee Schedule**: 19,356 priceable lines, 98 localities, conversion factor 33.4009 read from the file.

The product's whole claim is "this charge is X× Medicare." Until now it couldn't establish X. It can now, and it shows the arithmetic.

The engine ships in `backend/pfs/` and the data in `backend/data/cms/`, so a fresh clone prices with no external service, no API key, and no network.

## What changes for callers

**A rate depends on where and when.** `/api/upload` now accepts `state` (or `locality_id`), `setting`, and `date_of_service`.

```bash
curl -F "file=@backend/sample_bill.txt" -F "user_id=1" \
     -F "state=AL" -F "date_of_service=2026-03-14" \
     http://localhost:5000/api/upload
```

Same office visit, same day: **$125.23 in Alabama, $166.40 in San Francisco.**

**A line can have no benchmark, and says why** — statutory exclusion, not valid under this schedule, unknown code, ambiguous state, or a date outside the loaded release. Those lines contribute nothing to `total_savings`, so an unpriceable charge can never inflate a savings claim.

**Every priced line carries its derivation**, and it now appears in the appeal letter as the basis for each figure:

```
- Basis: CPT 99214, ALABAMA (10112-AL-00), non_facility, DOS 2026-03-14:
         (1.9200 + 1.7500 + 0.0792) x 33.4009 = $125.23 [2026-RVU26C]
```

That's the difference between a number a claims administrator can check and one they can dismiss.

**New:** `GET /api/localities/<state>`. 36 of 53 states contain exactly one Medicare locality, so the state settles the rate. The other 17 need a specific one — this is how a caller finds it.

## Two fixes along the way

**OCR is now an optional import.** `pytesseract` was imported at module scope, so the API wouldn't boot at all without Tesseract installed — including on a fresh clone. Text bills now work regardless, and `/api/health` reports whether OCR is available.

**`/api/health` reports the rate source** — release, conversion factor, line and locality counts, dates covered. If the CMS files are missing it says so rather than silently serving unpriced results.

## Verification

Four-line sample bill, end to end:

| Code | Charged | Medicare | × | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 99214 | $340.00 | $125.23 | 2.72 | flagged |
| 71046 | $210.00 | $29.60 | 7.09 | flagged |
| 80053 | $95.00 | — | — | no benchmark — PFS status `X`, statutory exclusion |
| 93000 | $145.00 | $13.95 | 10.39 | flagged |

Variance $526.22. Appeal letter cites the schedule version per line.

## Scope

Physician fee schedule only — professional services. Hospital facility charges price under OPPS (outpatient) and DRGs (inpatient), which are different systems; comparing a facility line to PFS is the wrong benchmark and this does not pretend otherwise.

items.title: perf(engine): stop building AOF records when there is no log
items.body:
`docs/benchmarks.md` carried v0.2 numbers while v0.3 had put the AOF into the
commit path. I assumed persistence-off was unchanged and said so. Measuring it
was the point.

## The assumption was wrong

```
benchmark                          documented     now     delta
BenchmarkEngineSet                      32.22    49.81     +55%   <-- with no log attached
BenchmarkStoreGetHit                    11.00    11.23      +2%
BenchmarkReadCommand                   106.10   105.70      -0%
BenchmarkEngineParallelMixed           194.70   187.50      -4%
```

Everything else was inside noise. `EngineSet` was 55% slower **with persistence
switched off entirely**.

The cause was an argument evaluated whether or not it was used. Every mutation
called `commit(aof.DeriveSet(...), apply)`, and Go builds that record before the
call gets far enough to discover there is no log to put it in. Deriving inside
the commit helpers, after the nil check, brings it to **41.9 ns**.

## The remaining ten nanoseconds are deliberate

The mutation methods wrap their locked section in a closure so the durability
wait is structurally outside the lock. That closure carries two `defer`s and so
is not inlined, and escape analysis confirms nothing heap-allocates — the cost
is the call frame.

Removing it would recover the time and give up the ordering that has `guard` run
*after* the unlock, without which a panic could leave `onFatal` deadlocked
against a held lock. Ten nanoseconds against the 108 ns it takes to decode the
command that asked for the write is not that trade. If v0.5's end-to-end work
disagrees, it will disagree with a number.

## Persistence had no benchmarks at all

Which is why none of this surfaced. Four now exist, separating what this code
costs from what a device costs:

| | ns/op | |
|---|---|---|
| `EngineSet` | 41.9 | no log |
| `EngineSetLoggedEverysec` | 946 | + handoff to the writer, wait for `write()` |
| `EngineSetLoggedAlways` | 1 001 | + wait for `Sync()` |
| `EngineSetLoggedToDisk` | 3 678 964 | a real `fsync` per write |
| `EngineSetLoggedToDiskParallel` | 756 653 | the same, writers in flight |

Most of the in-process cost is the goroutine handoff, not encoding. And `fsync`
dominates by four orders of magnitude — any reasoning about durability that
starts from the nanosecond figures is reasoning about the wrong number.

## Group commit now has a measurement, not just a claim

3.7 ms serially against 757 µs with writers in flight, about **4.8×**, because
writers waiting on the same `Sync` share the syscall. Spec §6.6 says this
follows from the construction rather than from a separate mechanism. Nothing had
checked it until now.

## Also

`docs/benchmarks.md` says up front that nothing in it is carried over from an
earlier version — carrying numbers forward is exactly what let a 55% regression
sit unnoticed for a release.

items.title: refactor(redact): scan assignments by index instead of re-matching fragments
items.body:
**No behaviour change.** Groundwork for #53 and #54, both of which need a rule to know *where* its match sits, not just what it matched.

## Why

`ReplaceAllStringFunc` hands the callback only the matched text, so both assignment rules re-ran the pattern against that fragment to recover their capture groups. Three problems:

1. Wasteful — the pattern runs twice per match.
2. Subtly wrong — a pattern can split an isolated fragment differently than it split the same text in context.
3. No position — a rule cannot inspect the byte *before* its match. Checking the character before a `{` is exactly what #53 needs to tell a YAML flow mapping from a parameter expansion.

`rewriteMatches` walks `FindAllStringSubmatchIndex` and rebuilds the string, so callbacks get real submatch indices.

Matching semantics are unchanged because the pattern is still applied to the **whole input** — anchors like `^` under `(?m)` still see real line starts. A naive "search the remaining slice from offset p" loop would have broken exactly that, which is why this uses `FindAll` rather than an offset loop.

## Verified as a no-op, not asserted as one

A differential harness rendered **every** corpus input at both redaction levels on this branch and on `682717b`, comparing byte for byte:

```
2258 renderings — identical digests
```

Every pinned expectation in the package is also unchanged. That self-checking property is the whole reason for splitting this from the behaviour change that follows: if anything shifted, the refactor would be wrong.

## Benchmark

Added over the megabyte log path `capsule.go:142` redacts wholesale, since cost on large inputs was the risk raised when planning this. Time is neutral within run-to-run noise; allocations improve because the pattern is no longer re-run per match:

| 539 KiB, default | B/op | allocs/op |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | 23.7 MB | 165,327 |
| this branch | 16.0 MB | 135,189 |

## Verification

- `FuzzRedactString` clean over **9.7M executions**
- Full gate: build, vet, staticcheck, `-race`, gofmt, whole suite. Coverage **71.6%** (floor 70.4)

## Next

#53 (`{token: secret}`) and #54 (a declined match consuming its span, hiding a nested secret) build on this. #54 additionally needs re-scanning inside a declined span, which `FindAll` alone does not permit — that part comes with the behaviour change.

## Summary

Fixes issue #156: novelty scoring compared against the wrong benchmark king and ignored SVF state.

## Root cause

`_compute_novelty()` iterated `leaderboard["benchmarks"]` and used the **first** king found (dict order dependent), not the king for the benchmark under evaluation. It also compared raw `head.select()` on bare prompts without applying the king's SVF scales.

## Fix approach

- `_king_submission_dir()` — lookup reigning submission for the **current benchmark** only
- `_routing_decisions()` — collect turn-1 routes via `policy.decide()` on the `QUERY:\n` transcript envelope
- Configure king's full θ (head + SVF) before comparing; use `trinity.novelty.novelty_score()`

## Impact

- Novelty (5% of composite) now reflects true routing diversity vs the correct benchmark king
- Multi-benchmark leaderboard state no longer skews novelty by iteration order

## Tests

Added `tests/test_pr_eval_novelty.py` (benchmark-scoped king lookup + transcript routing).

## Risks / tradeoffs

- Complements open PR #135 (same QUERY transcript for cached eval); this PR is novelty-only
- Novelty scores may shift when kings differ per benchmark or SVF diverges from head-only comparison

items.title: Give CDEB its schemas and a verifier that owns the whole study tree
items.body:
Closes #443. CDEB-01 — the first infrastructure ticket of the protocol landed in #442.

## What lands

**Six schemas** in `bench/cdeb/schemas/`, all `additionalProperties: false`, all requiring the explicit `benchmark: "cdeb-v1"` discriminator:

| schema | describes |
|---|---|
| `result` | the canonical measured row (PRD §19.2), every field required |
| `evaluator` | the sealed evaluator output (§12.4) — no free-form score is representable |
| `attempt` | one attempt with its terminal state (§10) |
| `study` | the public freeze manifest (§18.1), thresholds pinned as constants |
| `candidate` | a registry entry (§3.2) — `natural_record` and `benchmark_authored` are consts |
| `task` | sealed-task metadata with the §4.8 reviewer attestation |

**`bench/cdeb/verify.mjs`** — the recursive verifier of §21.1, and **CI integration**: `npm run bench:verify` now chains the legacy gate and this one. The CI yaml invokes the npm script, verified, so nothing bypasses it.

## The design inversion, stated

The legacy gate is deliberately **default-in** over flat `bench/results/*.jsonl` because its failure mode was a file nobody registered (#392). CDEB's failure mode is the opposite — an analysis surface discovering inputs it was never meant to read. #441 showed the M5 analyzer glob 1,835 rows from four experiments and nearly pass its own stopping rule on the contamination.

So in a CDEB study **every entry is accounted for or the study fails**, and classification is the explicit `benchmark` field — `schema_version` is never reused as a skip discriminator (§21.2).

## Derived fields are recomputed, not trusted (§14.7)

- `total_token_volume` against the raw category sum
- `decision_safe_success` against `stop_reason` + evaluator fields — a row claiming a safe success on a timeout fails whatever its schema-valid shape says

And a `RESULT.json` sitting beside missing expected rows fails as *"a verdict from an incomplete matrix"* — the artifact the analyzer must never produce (§22.6).

## One dependency gotcha

The schemas declare draft 2020-12; `ajv`'s default entry ships only the draft-07 meta-schema and refuses them at compile time. `Ajv2020` from `ajv/dist/2020.js`, with the reason at the import. Weakening six schemas to fit a meta-schema would have been backwards.

## Tests — 11, structured as control + single mutation

The clean study passes (the control), and each failure case is that same valid row with exactly one thing broken — so a passing case proves the verifier caught *that* defect, not an accident of the fixture: empty study, unknown file, invalid row, wrong `benchmark`, token-sum mismatch, derived mismatch, simulated row, duplicate id, missing-row-with-verdict. All drive the real verifier as a subprocess, because the acceptance criteria are exit codes CI will see.

## Verification

- Full suite: **95 files, 2196 passed**, 1 skipped.
- `npm run bench:verify` green with both verifiers chained (legacy: 1,592 rows in 14 files; CDEB: no studies yet, exits 0).
- `test/dogfood.test.ts` re-run after committing: 9 passed.

items.title: feat(bench): stale-read scenario for session-start (session 2)
items.body:
Session 1 shipped the `session-start` stale-read fix with no test, on the reading that the benchmark harness could not stage a mid-run change without a timer. That reading was wrong. `benchmarks/lifecycle` already ships `gh-mock/gh`, a stand-in placed first on PATH and configured by env, and the same shape applied to `git` solves it exactly.

`git-mock/git` forwards every invocation to the real git and, after the first `fetch` returns, pushes a branch to the bare remote. Counting fetches is what makes it deterministic; a sleep would race the agent's reading speed. It takes `GIT_MOCK_REAL` as an absolute path, because the shim is first on PATH and cannot resolve `git` by name, and the drift step uses that path throughout so the shim never recurses into itself.

The scenario discriminates on the session number rather than the branch base. Testing the base does not work: step 7's own option text runs `git fetch` before `git switch -c`, so even a skill that never re-reads ends up branching off a current ref. The number is computed before the question is asked and never revisited, so it is where a stale snapshot survives into the outcome, and it is what actually went wrong in aboard when two sessions both picked 41. Logs run through session 5 with no session branches, the shim lands `feature/session-6-concurrent`, and a stale skill mints 6 while a re-reading one mints 7.

`assert.sh` exits 2 on a void run, where the drift never landed. That distinction carries weight here: with no drift, the agent never met the condition, and 6 is the answer a correct skill and a broken harness both produce. Reporting that as a pass would be worse than having no test.

Mechanics are verified against hand-staged state: void exits 2, a `session-6` branch exits 1, a `session-7` branch exits 0, the shim fires once on the first fetch, handles `git -C <path> fetch` from an unrelated cwd, and does not trigger on non-fetch calls. The agent leg has not been run, so `scenario.md` records the baseline as pending rather than claiming a pass the other five scenarios have earned.

The session log also records why the prose-mint release did not happen. `prose-mint-v0.1.1` was tagged and pushed on 2026-07-27; the workflow ran, the build passed, and publish failed with `invalid-publisher` because PyPI has no Trusted Publisher registered for the project. The pipeline needs no change, and the next release should be 0.2.0 rather than a retry, since a feature landed after that tag.

Gate: 145 tests pass, shellcheck clean over both the manifest's targets and the three new scripts, bulk scan 4 files with 0 flagged lines.

items.title: feat: silent-wrong-action-rate benchmark (screen-verify vs effect-verify on MockMed faults)
items.body:
## What

Turns the #63 transactional fault-class matrix (`tests/test_effect_fault_matrix.py`) into a **measured, publishable metric** — the *silent wrong-action rate* instrument (`docs/validation/SILENT_WRONG_ACTION_RATE.md`) pointed at our OWN runtime. No competitor runs, no paid API, **no model calls**, localhost only.

For each MockMed fault scenario (`mockmed.fault_server`) the benchmark runs N times and records three **independent** judgments per run:

1. **Ground truth** — computed straight off the system-of-record store (before vs after), never from an oracle. Correct = exactly one `p1`/`Triage` encounter with this run's note and no pre-existing row destroyed.
2. **Screen oracle** (the weak, vision-style check) — the documented `app.js` saved-banner rule applied to the **real** server response(s).
3. **Effect oracle** — the #63 `RestRecordVerifier` consequential-save contract (`record_written` exactly once AND `field_equals` on the note) against `GET /api/db`.

Numbers are REAL — every run drives the fault server and reads back the store; nothing is hardcoded.

## Measured result (n=10/scenario, 90 runs)

| metric | screen-verify | effect-verify (#63) |
|---|---|---|
| silent-wrong-action rate (wrong effect ∧ oracle says success, all runs) | **55.6%** (50/90) | **0.0%** (0/90) |
| undetected-wrong rate (oracle says success \| wrong effect occurred) | **83.3%** | **0.0%** |
| false-abort rate (oracle halts \| effect correct) | 33.3% | 0.0% |

The five silent classes under screen-verify: `partial`, `optimistic`, `duplicate`, `double`, `stale` — each PASSes the screen while the record is wrong; effect-verify refutes all five. Effect-verify also rescues the `timeout` false-abort (row landed, screen reported failure) into a correct CONFIRMED.

## Files (all NEW — no edits to replayer/ir/resolver/compiler)

- `openadapt_flow/benchmark/silent_wrong_action.py` — benchmark + CLI (`python -m openadapt_flow.benchmark.silent_wrong_action --out ... --n ...`), emits `results.json`, `SILENT_WRONG_ACTION.md`, and a chart via `chart_fonts` (repo convention).

items.body:
## Summary

The posture section asserted **"Dependabot security updates: enabled"**. That was true for `mvl` and `mvl-spec`. The other six had it off — so the policy claimed a control most of the organisation did not have.

Found while verifying the previous PR's own claims, one commit after merging it. An unverified control claim inside the section whose entire purpose is honest posture.

## Changes

Enabled Dependabot alerts + security updates on all six repos that lacked it, and rewrote the line to state what is true.

| Repo | Secret scanning | Push protection | Dependabot |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mvl`, `mvl-spec` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (already) |
| `tree-sitter-mvl`, `examples`, `homebrew-mvl`, `mvl-lang.github.io`, `.github` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ **now** |
| `benchmark` | ✅ | ❌ deliberate | ✅ **now** |

## Correction to the previous PR's reasoning

[#2](https://github.com/mvl-lang/.github/pull/2) implied `benchmark` should be excluded from Dependabot because it would bump `log4j` and break the Log4Shell reproduction. **That was asserted, not checked, and it is wrong.**

`benchmark` declares **no dependency manifests of any kind** — no `pom.xml`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, or gradle file. Confirmed via `git ls-files`. The CVE reproductions are self-contained source files; `CVE-2021-44228_log4shell/vulnerable.java` imports `org.apache.logging.log4j` but the jar is never declared as a dependency, and its `Makefile` deliberately refuses to automate the download:

> ```
> # NOTE: Running vulnerable.java requires Log4j 2.x < 2.17.0
> # This is intentionally NOT automated due to the danger of
> # actually having vulnerable Log4j in the environment.
> ```

Dependabot has nothing to parse there — which is why the repo reports zero alerts. It is now enabled so that a manifest added later is covered from the start, and the policy says exactly that rather than implying active coverage.

**The push-protection exception stands**, on different and verified grounds: secret scanning reads source files, and the JNDI and prompt-injection payloads live in source where they plausibly match credential patterns.

## Testing

- [x] All 8 public repos re-queried after the change: `dependabot_security_updates: enabled` everywhere
- [x] `vulnerability-alerts` confirmed on for all 8 (the prerequisite for security updates)
- [x] Open Dependabot alerts counted per repo: **0** everywhere
- [x] Open secret-scanning alerts counted per repo: **0** everywhere
- [x] Absence of dependency manifests in `benchmark` verified against `git ls-files`, not the working tree
- [ ] No code changed

## Related

Third instance this session of the same error class — asserting a plausible mechanism without executing anything that could contradict it. That is the thesis of [mvl#2050](https://github.com/mvl-lang/mvl/issues/2050) (ADR-0060), here applied to my own security policy.

items.title: fix(kube-bench): audit a managed cluster against its own CIS benchmark
items.body:
Closes https://github.com/draugr-dev/draugr/issues/403.

## The bug

kube-bench consults its platform detection **only when neither flag is set** ([`cmd/common.go`](https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/blob/main/cmd/common.go), `getBenchmarkVersion`):

```go
if isEmpty(benchmarkVersion) && isEmpty(kubeVersion) && !isEmpty(platform.Name) {
    benchmarkVersion = getPlatformBenchmarkVersion(platform)
}
```

Draugr always passed `--version`, to stop the tool falling back to Kubernetes 1.18 and auditing against `cis-1.6`. That is right for a vanilla cluster and, it turns out, a guarantee of the opposite failure everywhere else: **every managed cluster fell through to the generic benchmark.**

## Why it isn't a near-miss

Measured on a live cluster, same `--targets policies`:

| benchmark | checks | numbered |
|---|---|---|
| `cis-1.12` | 34 | `5.1.1`, `5.1.10`, … |
| `eks-1.8.0` | 23 | `4.1.1`, `4.1.10`, … |
| `gke-1.9.0` | 20 | `4.1.1`, `4.1.2`, … |

**Different rule ids entirely.** So on EKS the report cited `cis/5.x` checks that do not exist in the EKS benchmark, failed the cluster for control-plane settings a managed provider does not expose, and skipped the provider checks that were the point. A `config.exclude` rule written against one could never match the other.

## The fix

The distribution comes out of the `GitVersion` Draugr already fetches (`v1.30.4-eks-a737599` → `eks`), using **kube-bench's own expression** — the aim is to reach the same conclusion the tool would, so a looser pattern that finds a platform kube-bench will not is worse than none.

| cluster | flags passed | benchmark chosen by |
|---|---|---|
| vanilla (`v1.34.0`) | `--version 1.34` | kube-bench's version mapping |
| recognized platform | *neither* | kube-bench's platform mapping |
| `benchmark` set | `--benchmark <value>` | you |

A build suffix is not automatically a platform: `v1.31.0-rc.1` parses exactly like `v1.30.4-eks-a737599`, so only suffixes kube-bench actually maps count and a release candidate stays vanilla.

### The output is the guarantee, not the input

Withholding the flags hands the choice to a tool with its own silent fallback — the same 1.18 one. So the benchmark kube-bench **reports having used** is checked against the detected platform before any finding is built. A run that audited the wrong standard is a failed scan, not a finding-free pass.

```
kube-bench audited against "cis-1.6", but this is a eks cluster and its benchmark starts
with "eks-". The result would describe the wrong standard. Set
controllers.infrastructure.benchmark to the config you want
```

## Scope

**Read-only scanner only.** `kube-bench-job` never passed `--version`, so it already reaches the platform benchmark — and in-cluster, kube-bench's detection is the reliable one (it is the only place AKS and RKE can be identified at all). Left alone deliberately rather than overlooked.

OpenShift is not detected: kube-bench identifies it by running `oc`, not from the version string, so this scanner cannot reach the same conclusion. `benchmark` covers it.

## Verified

- Benchmark prefixes read from kube-bench's actual `cfg/` tree, not guessed — two of my first guesses (`k3s-cis-`, `rke-cis-`) were wrong.
- `platformFrom` tested against **real version strings** from each provider, plus the cases that must stay vanilla (kind, a release candidate, an unknown distribution).
- `verifyBenchmark` tested both ways, including the exact stale-default case (`cis-1.6` on an `eks` cluster) and `rke-` vs `rke2-`.
- **Live regression check** on a v1.34 `kind` cluster: still 29 findings via `cis-1.12`, unchanged.
- `make gate` clean.

The managed path cannot be verified locally — `kind` emits no platform token. The mechanism is covered by unit tests against real provider version strings, and the output check means a wrong benchmark fails loudly rather than reporting. Worth a run against a real EKS or GKE cluster when one is available.

items.title: Compute BENCHMARK_GT's conclusions instead of asserting them, and regenerate what was stale
items.body:
Follow-up to #8. The scaffold re-run landed and worked; these are two problems that surfaced while checking it.

## The re-run verified

| | |
|---|---|
| random rows changed | **0 of 204** — cache preserved as intended |
| scaffold rows changed | **156 of 183** |
| new rows | **21**, all ShapeGGen scaffold — those cells used to crash |
| MUTAG scaffold split | `47 scaffolds over 188 molecules, 89.4% in multi-member groups` |
| SynthMotifs | `0.0% grouped` → **DEGENERATE** warning fired |

The leak had been inflating shift results: BBBP scaffold accuracy 0.98 → 0.83, AUC 0.966 → 0.925. The pathological BACE cell (acc 0.005, AUC 0.105) is gone — now 0.440 / 0.698. Median across-seed sd on GT AUROC improved 0.052 → 0.042; MUTAG · GINE · PGExplainer · scaffold went from 0.670 ± 0.546 to 0.320 ± 0.077. Much of what looked like seed noise was the broken partition.

## 1. The report asserted conclusions it never computed

`BENCHMARK_GT.md`'s "What this shows" was a fixed paragraph claiming in-distribution "faithfulness and correctness agree… ρ near 1, no mismatch" and shift mismatch at "p < 0.001". Neither number was read back from the run, and both are false on this data — in-distribution MUTAG · GINE mismatches on all three faithfulness metrics with mean ρ = +0.20. That breaches the project's first hard rule.

Worse, the 3 August report carried **no in-distribution panel at all** and still described the contrast. `resolve_cells` accepted a partial match against `DEFAULT_CELLS`, `SynthMotifsXL` was not in this sweep, so that half vanished silently. It also broke the dissociation figure, which needs two regimes and got one — and `collect_figures` then copied the surviving figure from an earlier run's artifacts into `results/`, republishing a figure drawn from pre-fix data as this run's output with nothing to mark it.

Fixed:
- Conclusions are derived from the computed results, state the direction actually found, and say plainly when a run does **not** support the dissociation claim.
- The preferred cell set is taken only if it survives whole.
- `DEFAULT_CELLS` is MUTAG · GINE on both splits — same dataset and backbone either side, so the contrast isolates scaffold shift. MUTAG is the only ground-truth arm that is both molecular (BA-2Motifs, SynthMotifs and ShapeGGen have no Bemis–Murcko scaffold) and unsaturated (MolMotif sits at GT AUROC ≈0.99, where ranking attributors is noise around a ceiling).

items.title: fix(cargo): surface `rebuilt` so ok:true can't mask a stale no-op build (#946)
items.body:
## What

The daimonos `cargo build`/`check`/`clippy` tool set only `"ok": <cargo exit status>`, so a **no-op build** (cargo decides the tree is up-to-date and recompiles nothing) is indistinguishable from one that produced a fresh artifact. During #945 this returned `ok:true` on a **day-stale release binary**, and I nearly reported a wrong benchmark result off old code.

Now the result carries **`"rebuilt"`**: `true` iff ≥1 crate had `fresh:false` this run. So `ok:true, rebuilt:false` tells the caller "cargo was up-to-date, no new artifact" — the signal that was missing. It doesn't try to defeat cargo's fingerprint; it just makes the no-op observable so a build-then-run loop can notice.

## How

Refactors the `--message-format=json` parsing out of `cargo_diagnostics` into a **pure `parse_cargo_json(stdout) -> {errors, warnings, rebuilt}`**, and reports `rebuilt` in the build/check/clippy result. No change to errors/warnings behavior.

## Tests

Two pure unit tests: recompile-vs-no-op detection (`fresh:false` ⇒ `rebuilt`), and diagnostic collection with junk-line tolerance + span extraction. Full suite **664** pass, `clippy --all-targets -D warnings` clean (both run via real `cargo`), pre-commit gate clean.

## Context

Filed + root-caused in vikunja #946. Impact was low for CI/benchmark (they build via real `cargo` from clean trees) but a real trust hazard for build-via-MCP-then-run workflows.

items.title: fix(core): name the real fault when several addresses are passed
items.body:
> Supersedes #22, which GitHub auto-closed when its base branch (`fix/kind-allowed-values`, now merged as #21) was deleted. Same branch, rebased onto `dev`; the diff is unchanged.

## What changed

New `Error::MultipleAddresses(Vec<String>)` at exit 1. When `parse_lenient` cannot coerce its extra positionals and at least one of them looks like an address, it now says so and lists them, instead of joining everything into one string and blaming the path.

## Why

```
$ agentlens slice a.py#Foo b.py#Bar
agentlens: cannot read `a.py#Foo b.py#Bar` as an address: no file on disk matches its path
```

The variadic `<address>...` exists for coercion (`slice f.py 10 20` → `f.py#L10-L20`), not batching. But `--help` advertises `<address>...`, so the signature invites the mistake, and the error then blames the path — sending the caller hunting for a file that was never meant to exist.

Now:

```
agentlens: this command takes one address, but got 2: `a.py#Foo`, `b.py#Bar`
run each address in its own call
```

**A distinct variant, not reworded `AddressUnresolved`.** `Error::kind()` is the stable machine-readable field agents branch on instead of the prose. Reporting `address_unresolved` for an arity problem would make the JSON envelope lie, which is worse than the message being wrong.

## Benchmark failure class

n/a directly — but adjacent to a real one. The v0.1.0 eval found 67/339 agentlens calls were address-syntax errors; this makes one class of them self-correcting rather than misleading.

## Verification

- [x] `scripts/ci.sh` green locally — 134 tests
- [x] Snapshots regenerated and the diff read

Snapshot churn was **2 new, 0 modified**. That `error_unresolved_extra_arguments.txt` (`slice nowhere 1 20`) did *not* move is the load-bearing check: it proves the predicate does not fire on selector-shaped extras.

RED first — the tests did not compile, then failed with `blamed the path instead of the arity: ...` once the variant existed.

Regression fence, all passing before and after: `f.py 10 20`, `f.py 10`, `f.py Symbol`, `f.py:10-20`, `f.py::Sym`, bare `f.py`, plus `nowhere 1 20` and `f.py 1 x` still resolving to `AddressUnresolved`.

The predicate is consulted **only after `coerce` has already returned `None`**, so it is structurally incapable of turning a working rewrite into an error.

## Token-cost impact

None on success paths. On this error path the message is ~15 tokens longer and saves at least one wasted follow-up call.

## Deviations

No `#[allow(...)]` added.

**Batching deliberately not implemented.** `SliceMatch` is already a `Vec` (the `@overload` case), but the envelope emits a singular `"address"` and `Report.found` is a single `bool` — real batching needs a new envelope shape (`schema_version` break), a cross-address budget policy, a partial-success exit code, and N coercion notes, then the same again for `callers` and `packet`. That is a feature, not a defect fix. This change is forward-compatible: if batching lands later, `MultipleAddresses` simply stops being constructed.

`is_address()` deliberately not extended, so no `run 'agentlens help addresses'` hint is appended — that page documents grammar, not arity, and would send the caller somewhere that cannot help.

items.title: guard: multi-candidate did-you-mean, and the allocation bug behind it (#200)
items.body:
Closes the real remainder of #200. The issue read as unbuilt; most of it **already
shipped** (`Suggest` with Levenshtein ≤2, wired into all three violation
producers and both renderers). Two items genuinely remained — and measuring the
second found a defect neither the issue nor my own triage comment on it had right.

## 1. Multi-candidate

`Suggest` returned exactly one name. Now up to three, nearest first, ties broken
lexicographically so output stays deterministic. `Violation.Suggestion` (string)
→ `Suggestions` (`[]string`); the renderer joins them as
`did you mean "a" or "b"?`. When two names are equally plausible, one suggestion
made the agent guess.

## 2. A relative floor

A flat distance-2 threshold is too loose on short identifiers: two edits on a
three-character name have changed most of it, so `abc` drew a confident
suggestion of `xyc` — a *different name*, not a typo of this one. `withinFloor`
requires `2*dist <= len`, which only bites below four characters.

## 3. The bail-out the issue asked for is NOT here — measuring it found the real bug

The issue asked to "bail out on large sets." My own triage comment went further
and called the latency *"mostly theoretical — the inner loop is an int compare."*
**Both were wrong.** Benchmark on a realistic symbol set:

```
before:  ~4.0 ms/op   2,877,162 B/op   18,000 allocs/op
after:   ~1.2 ms/op       3,956 B/op       13 allocs/op
```

`levenshtein` allocated a fresh row **per character** of the probe, **per
candidate** — a 17-char name against ~1000 length-matched candidates allocated
~18,000 slices for *one* suggestion, a third of the hook's 12 ms budget spent
entirely on garbage. The length prune hides this in a unit test but not in
production: real codebases cluster name lengths, so most candidates survive the
prune and reach the distance loop.

Reusing a scratch row pair: **1385× fewer allocations, 727× less garbage, ~3×
faster.** A size cap would have capped the *symptom* and silently degraded
suggestions on exactly the large repos where they help most.

`suggest_bench_test.go` pins it. Watch `allocs/op` — that regresses long before
wall-clock does on a fast machine, which is why this went unnoticed.

## Test that caught its own author

`TestSuggest_ShortNameFloor` first asserted `foo`→`bar` is floor-rejected and
`id`→`ID` is kept. Both wrong: `foo`/`bar` is distance **3**, so `maxDist`
rejects it before the floor is ever consulted (the test exercised nothing), and
`id`/`ID` is distance **2**, not 1, so the floor correctly drops it. The doc
comment I wrote the test from carried the same error and is corrected.

## Verification

`go test ./... -race -cover` all ok · `go vet` clean · `gofmt -l` clean under the
go.mod-pinned go1.25.0. Guard coverage 93.0% → 93.1%. 3 new tests + 1 benchmark.

items.title: Phase 1.3 — Vigenère and Hill
items.body:
Adds the two ciphers the Phase 3 K4-proxy composites need. Completes Phase 1 except for 1.5 (republishing K3's corrected `solution` field).

## Vigenère delegates rather than duplicating

Vigenère is *exactly* Quagmire III over the unkeyed alphabet: with A–Z on both axes, "shift by the key letter's index in the alphabet" reduces to `c = (p + k) mod 26`. Verified against `ATTACKATDAWN` + `LEMON` → `LXFOPVEFRNHR`.

So the module delegates. A second copy of the shift arithmetic would be a second thing to keep correct, and the two would drift the first time either changed. What the module adds is naming and a default, so a caller building a composite need not know a Quagmire sits underneath.

The tests pin the *equivalence*, not just the behaviour — if the two ever diverge, delegation stops being safe and a test says so.

## Hill: invertibility is the interesting part

`c = Kp (mod 26)`, decryption by the adjugate inverse. The condition is `gcd(det, 26) == 1`, **not** `det != 0` — 26 is composite, so every even determinant and every multiple of 13 is singular. That's the trap randomly generated keys fall into, so `is_invertible` is exposed for Phase 3 to screen with. A test walks all 26 determinants and asserts invertibility tracks the gcd; another asserts the units are exactly the twelve residues coprime to 26.

`recover_key` implements the known-plaintext attack that Hill's linearity admits — what a Tier 4 solver would run against the `BERLIN`/`CLOCK` cribs under the Hill conjecture.

## Three real bugs caught in review

All would have produced *wrong benchmark data* rather than loud failures:

- **Non-square matrices were accepted.** `_validate_matrix` checked rows were equal length but never that the matrix was square, and `_apply`'s `zip` silently discarded extra columns. A 2×3 key encrypted, decrypted and round-tripped exactly like its 2×2 prefix — while the ground-truth label named a key that was never applied.
- **`recover_key` returned an unverified key.** Solving from `n` blocks is exact only if the pair is consistent, and a crib attack *guesses* at alignment, so inconsistency is the normal case. Corrupting one ciphertext letter returned `((2,2),(2,5))` for a true key of `((3,3),(2,5))`, silently. It now verifies against the whole ciphertext and reports that the alignment is probably wrong.
- **`recover_key` had a combinatorial cliff.** It scanned `C(blocks, size)` — a 4×4 key with 60 known blocks is 487,635 selections, measured at ~30s. Replaced with greedy rank selection over GF(2) and GF(13) (invertible mod 26 exactly when invertible mod both), one linear pass. Greedy isn't complete for matroid intersection, so a failure means "not found" rather than "absent", and the error says so.

Plus an API hazard: this module's second positional argument is the *key* while `quagmire`'s is the *alphabet keyword*. Over 500 random cases the two orderings agreed once — a positional mixup would silently mislabel dataset rows. `alphabet_keyword` is now keyword-only, so it's a `TypeError`.

## Test defects fixed too

- The `recover_key` property test **passed only on its committed seed** — 7 of 60 seeds would have failed. It now supplies enough blocks that success isn't luck, and is parametrised across seeds.
- The length test used `"A" * n`, which is the zero vector and a fixed point of *every* Hill key — it would have passed with the arithmetic entirely broken.
- The keyed-alphabet path, which is the one Phase 3 uses, had only a self-referential comparison against `quagmire`. It now has an independent reference implementation.

## Tests

221 → 244.

## Plan items

- [x] 1.3 Vigenère and Hill — all four boxes

Phase 1 is 18/21. Only **1.5** remains: K3's `solution` field on the Hub still says the geometry "is not asserted here", and 1.2 derived it.

items.title: fix(sweep): the per-query embed seam enforces one vector per text (#112)
items.body:
<!-- mirrored-from: jt-mchorse/embedding-model-shootout#pr-113 -->

Source: https://github.com/jt-mchorse/embedding-model-shootout/pull/113

`run_sweep` checked the corpus call's row count inline and left the per-query call — nine lines below, same duck-typed `Embedder` Protocol (D-004) — unguarded. `_reject_non_finite_vectors`'s docstring said the length check "already lives" at the embedder-output seam; that was true of one of the two.

## Two failures, verified firsthand on `main` (72a17da)

**Too few → raw `IndexError`.** `embedder.embed([q.text])[0]` on an empty list — the exact malformation the corpus guard exists for — indexes out of range. `sweep run` catches `ValueError`, not `IndexError`, so it escaped as a traceback at exit 1.

```
QUERY SEAM  -> IndexError: list index out of range
CORPUS SEAM -> ValueError: embedder returned 1 vectors for 2 texts
```

**Too many → a silently wrong benchmark.** `[0]` took the first row and asked no questions:

```
honest recall:        {1: 1.0, 5: 1.0, 10: 1.0}
extra-vector recall:  {1: 0.0, 5: 1.0, 10: 1.0}   ← no error, no warning
```

That second one is the one I'd flag. `_reject_non_finite_vectors` was added because a NaN component yields "plausible-but-wrong recall/NDCG" that the `SweepResult` range guard (#62) can't catch. This is the same corruption reached through arity instead of value, at the seam that check skipped.

## Why the seam is reachable

The five shipped SDK providers each assemble their output differently — `openai_provider` sorts `response.data` by `.index`, `cohere_provider` reads `response.embeddings.float`, `voyage` extends from `response.embeddings`, `bge`/`nomic` map over a numpy array. None checks that what came back has one row per input, so a truncated or partial batch response (rate limiting, a retried request, an SDK version change) lands here. The corpus path catches it for the batch call; the per-query path did not.

## What changed

`_require_one_vector_per_text`, applied at both seams. One helper rather than two inline checks, because the gap existed precisely because the two seams were separate expressions of the same contract.

**One thing I said I'd keep and didn't:** the corpus seam's message. It now names the embedder and the seam kind (`embedder 'openai/…' returned 1 vectors for 2 corpus texts; …`) instead of the bare `embedder returned 1 vectors for 2 texts`. Nothing in the tests, docs or README asserted the old wording, and sharing one message across both seams is the point of the helper — but it is a change, so it's worth stating rather than burying.

## On the tests

Nine tests. The one worth reading is `test_extra_vector_scored_the_wrong_recall_before_the_guard`: it anchors the guard to the **wrong number** rather than to an exception type, by performing exactly what the unguarded line did and asserting the wrong chunk comes back. Otherwise someone could later "fix" a regression here by widening a catch while the silent-corruption path quietly returns.

The lock parses `sweep.py` with `ast` and asserts one guard per `embedder.embed(...)` call site, rather than asserting the two known seams — which would go stale the moment a third is added, exactly how this gap appeared. It parses rather than greps because the guard's own docstring quotes the expression it replaced, and a text scan counts that prose as a call site (it did, on the first run).

One thing I caught while writing them, worth noting because it would have produced a green test that proved nothing: the CLI test's first fixture used short corpus texts, so `build_queries` exited 2 with `no corpus chunks have >= 6 words` — **the same exit code the test asserts**, for an entirely unrelated reason. It passed on the unfixed tree. The fixture now uses six-word chunks and the assertion pins the actual message, with a comment saying why.

Reverting `emb_shootout/sweep.py` fails six of the nine, verified before shipping.

Full suite 435 passed; `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` clean on 0.16.1, CI's unpinned version.

## Deferred

Verifying `self.dim` against the actual vector width. The Protocol documents "all vectors share `self.dim`" and nothing checks it — related, but a separate contract and a separate issue.

Closes #112

items.title: fix(bench): the other three arms refused every question too
items.body:
Follow-up to #244, which fixed the LOCOMO arm and flagged three siblings carrying the identical defect.

## The bug

`benchmarks/ladder/systems/recall_system.py`, `benchmarks/membench/recall_isolation.py` and `benchmarks/membench/recall_temporal.py` all called `trusted_search` with no policy. `TrustPolicy` defaults to strict, and a benchmark corpus has no generation and no published calibration, so each raised `TrustRefusal: INDEX_NOT_READY` before retrieval ran.

## The policy half alone would have been silently worse on two of them

Development mode with `calibration=None` means "no threshold exists at all", so `recall/trust.py` blanks every verdict to `unverified` and forces `abstained=False`. That breaks the two readings in opposite directions:

| Arm | Reads | Policy-only outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `recall_temporal`, ladder | `verdict == "ok"` | nothing clears the filter → cites nothing → **0.0000 everywhere** |
| `recall_isolation` | `result.abstained` | forced False → collapses to "did retrieval return anything" |

For `recall_temporal` that is indistinguishable from a validity layer that does not work, which is the exact failure that adapter was previously fixed for. For `recall_isolation`, a leak axis pinned near 1.0 cannot tell correct isolation from an adapter answering out of the wrong tenant.

So the two-part decision now lives in one place, `benchmarks/_trust.py`, instead of at four call sites. It normalises a `None` **calibration** and a `None` **policy**, because `None` is the spelling that reads like "use the default" while meaning the opposite in each case: `calibration=None` is "no threshold exists", and `policy=None` resolves through `None or TrustPolicy()` straight back to strict.

## Two more modules, found by auditing this change

- **`benchmarks/check_temporal_live.py`** — a **pre-registered** check whose P2 predicate *and* its P3 control are both read off `hit.verdict`. With verdicts blanked, P2 was structurally unreachable and P3 passed vacuously, so it printed "NOT live" and exited 1 whatever the validity layer did. The control that exists to prove the reference time reached the trust layer had become the thing certifying nothing was wrong.
- **`benchmarks/beam/ksweep.py`** — reads only hit text, so nothing it measures changes. Routed through the seam anyway, so "arms that happen not to read verdicts" stops being a category someone re-decides per module.

## Why the guard is a source scan

Every one of these adapters is unreachable from CI. The two mem-bench ones import `membench`, a separate repo `pyproject.toml` deliberately does not depend on; the LOCOMO one's tests need `fastembed`, absent from `[dev]`. **A behavioural test for any of them would be a test CI skips — the failure mode being closed, reproduced inside the guard meant to close it.**

`tests/test_bench_trust_policy.py` parses every module under `benchmarks/` and enforces both halves: no route to `trusted_search` by any of the five import spellings that bind it, and no `research_search` call without a calibration, counting a literal `calibration=None` as missing. No import, no database, no optional extra, and it covers arms that do not exist yet. Parsed rather than grepped, because these modules discuss `trusted_search` at length in prose.

## What the guard cannot do, stated in it

A calibration passed as a **variable** is unjudgeable from source. `benchmarks/beam/systems.py` writes `calibration=self._calibration`, which is `None` on any run without `--calibration`, and the rule reports it as compliant.

One consequence is worth naming, since that file's own docstring calls abstention "the single design decision this benchmark exists to price": on a default run its `if result.abstained: return []` is unreachable, so **that category currently measures nothing**. Not changed here — it is a deliberate, documented arm with a disclosed uncalibrated default, and its own decision to make.

`importlib` is likewise undetectable, and documented as an accepted limit: this guard catches the ordinary omission that has now happened four times, not an adversary.

## Verification

- 176 tests pass across the eight affected files, against a dedicated container (not the shared `recall-db-1`). `ruff` and `mypy` clean.
- Both membench adapters, which CI cannot import, were exercised locally against the installed `membench`: development policy, explicit 0.50 calibration, `now=` still threaded.
- Written test-first: the import rule was watched failing and named exactly the three offenders; the calibration rule named exactly the two new ones.
- Every guard mutation-tested after each audit round — reverting any adapter, aliasing the import, or writing `calibration=None` all turn it red.
- Three rounds of adversarial bug-audit, eight findings, all fixed. Including one against my own guard: it originally accepted `calibration=None` and pinned that acceptance in a test whose comment claimed `_trust` would normalise it, which is false for exactly the calls the rule judges.

items.title: fix(sweep): the per-query embed seam enforces one vector per text (#112)
items.body:
`run_sweep` checked the corpus call's row count inline and left the per-query call — nine lines below, same duck-typed `Embedder` Protocol (D-004) — unguarded. `_reject_non_finite_vectors`'s docstring said the length check "already lives" at the embedder-output seam; that was true of one of the two.

## Two failures, verified firsthand on `main` (72a17da)

**Too few → raw `IndexError`.** `embedder.embed([q.text])[0]` on an empty list — the exact malformation the corpus guard exists for — indexes out of range. `sweep run` catches `ValueError`, not `IndexError`, so it escaped as a traceback at exit 1.

```
QUERY SEAM  -> IndexError: list index out of range
CORPUS SEAM -> ValueError: embedder returned 1 vectors for 2 texts
```

**Too many → a silently wrong benchmark.** `[0]` took the first row and asked no questions:

```
honest recall:        {1: 1.0, 5: 1.0, 10: 1.0}
extra-vector recall:  {1: 0.0, 5: 1.0, 10: 1.0}   ← no error, no warning
```

That second one is the one I'd flag. `_reject_non_finite_vectors` was added because a NaN component yields "plausible-but-wrong recall/NDCG" that the `SweepResult` range guard (#62) can't catch. This is the same corruption reached through arity instead of value, at the seam that check skipped.

## Why the seam is reachable

The five shipped SDK providers each assemble their output differently — `openai_provider` sorts `response.data` by `.index`, `cohere_provider` reads `response.embeddings.float`, `voyage` extends from `response.embeddings`, `bge`/`nomic` map over a numpy array. None checks that what came back has one row per input, so a truncated or partial batch response (rate limiting, a retried request, an SDK version change) lands here. The corpus path catches it for the batch call; the per-query path did not.

## What changed

`_require_one_vector_per_text`, applied at both seams. One helper rather than two inline checks, because the gap existed precisely because the two seams were separate expressions of the same contract.

**One thing I said I'd keep and didn't:** the corpus seam's message. It now names the embedder and the seam kind (`embedder 'openai/…' returned 1 vectors for 2 corpus texts; …`) instead of the bare `embedder returned 1 vectors for 2 texts`. Nothing in the tests, docs or README asserted the old wording, and sharing one message across both seams is the point of the helper — but it is a change, so it's worth stating rather than burying.

## On the tests

Nine tests. The one worth reading is `test_extra_vector_scored_the_wrong_recall_before_the_guard`: it anchors the guard to the **wrong number** rather than to an exception type, by performing exactly what the unguarded line did and asserting the wrong chunk comes back. Otherwise someone could later "fix" a regression here by widening a catch while the silent-corruption path quietly returns.

The lock parses `sweep.py` with `ast` and asserts one guard per `embedder.embed(...)` call site, rather than asserting the two known seams — which would go stale the moment a third is added, exactly how this gap appeared. It parses rather than greps because the guard's own docstring quotes the expression it replaced, and a text scan counts that prose as a call site (it did, on the first run).

One thing I caught while writing them, worth noting because it would have produced a green test that proved nothing: the CLI test's first fixture used short corpus texts, so `build_queries` exited 2 with `no corpus chunks have >= 6 words` — **the same exit code the test asserts**, for an entirely unrelated reason. It passed on the unfixed tree. The fixture now uses six-word chunks and the assertion pins the actual message, with a comment saying why.

Reverting `emb_shootout/sweep.py` fails six of the nine, verified before shipping.

Full suite 435 passed; `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` clean on 0.16.1, CI's unpinned version.

## Deferred

Verifying `self.dim` against the actual vector width. The Protocol documents "all vectors share `self.dim`" and nothing checks it — related, but a separate contract and a separate issue.

Closes #112

items.title: feat(changelog): /changelog on the design layer — the SPINE case, and the band finally had its set
items.body:
Eighth switchable route, and structurally unlike anything before it. `/docs` is a hierarchy and §5 answers it by moving depth onto enclosure. A changelog has **no depth**: it is N records of one shape, so the load-bearing rule is **G** — machine identity at the edges (month, area), human content in the middle, fixed rhythm, a colour edge for *identification* and never status.

## The dominant is a DATE, not a count

"N changes" is the obvious dominant. It is refused twice over:

- a count of entries **changes with every release**, so a register row for it would be stale by design — and a register whose rows go stale on a schedule stops being re-verified at all;
- it would pass the claim gate **by coincidence**. Nine entries today and `9` is unregistered; at twelve it would silently start passing because `12` is the Starter credit pack. That is the digit collision the register documents as a known limit, used on purpose.

So the dominant is **the most recent date** — a real measurement of what a reader came to check, read as a *date* rather than a quantity — with its condition beside it: the span covered, and the copy's own *"dates are when the change reached production."*

## The band earned its place without argument

On `/` the band had to be **given** a fact (#411). Here E.2's requirement was already in the data: the tags are a closed set and their entry counts are its composition, so **band count = cardinality, band width = share**, tallied at render.

The counts are **not printed** — the widths say it, the rows are all on the page for anyone who wants to count (C.3's *"derivable on the surface"*), and printing them would put seven unregistered numerals on a public surface to repeat what the picture already states. The legend is the second channel rule C requires, and **the band's colour index and each spine's edge colour are the same number**, so the picture and the list are one statement rather than two that happen to agree.

A tag beyond the data-colour set renders **unpainted rather than aliased** — rule D.2 for a set living in two files — exercised with a fabricated seven-tag overflow rather than waiting for a real seventh area.

No mode column: rule D is the notation for facts that can be **unknown**, and a shipped change is not in doubt. Nothing moves: it is a record.

## ⚠️ One real find in inherited copy

The claim gate reddened on **`135`** — *"the detection benchmark grew from 135 to 534 packages"*. `135` is a prior benchmark size with **no row and no source**, and it has been on the live `/changelog` all along; no numeral gate had ever read that page.

**Removed rather than registered**, deliberately: the news is the growth and `534` is registered, while a register row for a superseded size would make a stale figure quotable — and the register's own header records that quoting the wrong benchmark size has already happened twice (284, 479). The sentence loses nothing a reader needs.

Also the entity trap again, in a new assertion: `esc()` writes `What's new`, and a raw digit check on the masthead read the entity's own digits as a figure. Decoded before checking — **model the rendered text, not the markup.**

## The #422 refactor paid immediately

This route is **one row** in `SWITCHABLE_PAGES`, typed against `SwitchableRoute`. `resolveStandalonePage` did not change at all.

## Verified

2 573 unit tests · lint clean at the CI scope · design gate **27/27** with `/changelog` staged in both substrates · switchover **190/190 in both schemes**, `/changelog` sweeping 59 nodes at min **6.80:1** light and **8.40:1** dark.

Built, **not flipped** — and per #417 the flip needs a **rebuild**, not just the variable.

items.title: fix(arenabench): flip replay never applied a patch where it was taken
items.body:
`replay_flip` shipped in #1533 without ever being run. Running it against real containers found **three bugs, and every one produced the same silent wrong answer**: `flip_index=None` — which an operator reads as *"the agent never solved it"* rather than *"this could not be measured"*.

## The three

**1. `git apply` ran inside the probe container.** A task image is not guaranteed to ship git. The capture side only gets away with assuming it because Stella's adapter installs git into the *task* container; a replay probe is a fresh container from the pristine image and gets no such help.

```
snapshot 4: patch did not apply: sh: 1: git: not found
flip_index=None  probes=3 unknown=2
```

**2. Patches were applied at `/`.** Snapshots are captured with `--work-tree=<workspace>`, so their paths are workspace-relative. Even where git existed, every file landed in the wrong place.

**3. The workspace was re-probed instead of recorded.** This is the worst of the three, because **nothing failed** — the patch applied *cleanly to the wrong directory*. Capture probes a container the agent has been living in; replay probes a fresh one from the pristine image, and a directory the agent created exists in the first and not the second. `SnapshotEntry` now carries the workspace it was taken of, and replay uses it; the probe is only a fallback for manifests written before the field existed.

## The fix

Patches are applied **host-side**, where `git` is a checked precondition, into the recorded workspace, then copied back. Host `git` is required up front rather than discovered per-probe, because a run of unknowns summarises to the same misleading `flip_index=None`.

## Plus a preflight for the same failure class

The verifier reports its verdict by writing `/logs/verifier/reward.txt` into a bind mount. If the runtime cannot see that directory, no reward ever appears and every probe reads "did not pass". A VM-backed Docker shares only some host paths — measured:

```
host dir:  /var/folders/…/tmp.JtOiWATaBM   in container: (empty)
home dir:  /Users/…/.arenabench/…          in container: marker.txt
```

`/var/folders` is exactly where `pytest`'s `tmp_path` lives, so this is easy to hit. One container start now converts a silent, wrong benchmark number into a sentence naming the fix.

## Witness

`tests/test_replay_docker.py` drives capture → replay end to end against a synthetic task whose flip point is **known in advance**, and asserts `unknown == 0`, that the flip lands at or after the real solution, and that bisection probed fewer snapshots than it examined. It fails on each of the three bugs.

```
flip_index=3  flip_elapsed=6.33  wasted_elapsed=4.19
probes=3 unknown=0 snapshots=6
```

Synthetic task, so no dataset, no credentials, no spend. Skipped without docker+git, so CI pays nothing. Also adds unit coverage for the workspace round-trip and for manifests written before the field existed.

`pytest` and `ruff check` are clean by exit code.

## Why this kept happening

All three bugs, the bind-mount trap, and the `AuthenticationError` gap in #1534 are one shape: **absence of measurement rendering as a measured value**. In a benchmark that is never neutral — it always favours somebody. `bisect_first_pass` already treats an un-runnable probe as `None` rather than `False` for this reason; these fixes extend the same discipline to the layer underneath it.

## Summary by Sourcery

Ensure replay flip applies patches correctly and fails early when measurement is impossible, so flip detection reports accurate results instead of silent unknowns.

New Features:
- Add a host-side patch application workflow for replay probes that uses the recorded workspace from snapshots.
- Introduce a preflight bind-mount check to verify the container runtime can expose the scratch directory and rewards to the host.

Bug Fixes:
- Fix replay flip misapplying patches inside the probe container, at the wrong path, and against a misdetected workspace, which previously surfaced as flip_index=None.
- Ensure manifests without an explicit workspace still load and fall back to probing instead of failing.

Enhancements:
- Extend SnapshotEntry to record the workspace path for each snapshot so capture and replay agree on where patches should apply.

Tests:
- Add an end-to-end Docker-based replay_flip test that covers the three patching bugs and validates flip detection behaviour.
- Add unit tests covering workspace round-tripping in manifests, including compatibility with manifests written before the workspace field existed.

items.title: manifest 0.63: not reported is not the same as not knowable (corrects 0.62)
items.body:
0.62 was shipped on a wrong finding. The benchmark scored agents as fabricating a measurement when they had correctly inferred FE(C2H4) on pure Au from a closed product slate: H2 + CO equals total_faradaic_efficiency to 0.0000, bounding the unreported channel at zero. Mass balance decides what no descriptor reports. The agents were right; the answer key was wrong.

0.62 encoded that mistake into the contract by telling agents that an unreported quantity means `insufficient`. That would train them to discard information a conservation constraint makes available, and over-caution is a failure mode we have already observed.

0.63: a quantity is available if reported, OR derivable from what is reported, OR obtained from a compute run. Only then is `insufficient` honest. The compliance check gets the matching exemption. 262 tests pass.

items.title: fix(metallib): key the cache on mlx working-tree contents, not just HEAD
items.body:
## Summary `scripts/fetch-metallib.sh` keyed its cache on the mlx submodule's **HEAD commit** plus the deployment target. Kernel work happens in the **working tree** long before it is committed, so any uncommitted change to mlx kernels silently reused a metallib built from *different sources* than the host code dispatching into it. ## Why this is a correctness bug, not a cache-hygiene nit Hit while patching `qmm_t_impl`'s `M` parameter (`const constant int&` → `const int`). The host encoded the argument one way; the cached metallib expected the other. Result: **the GPU wedged at 0% CPU with no error message**, which presented as a hung test suite and cost a debugging cycle chasing a phantom regression. The worse failure mode is silent: a benchmark run in that state reports confident numbers for kernels that were never built. Any uncommitted-kernel A/B measured through this script was untrustworthy. ## Fix Fold uncommitted state into the cache key — tracked diffs plus untracked file contents, hashed and appended as a `-w` suffix: ``` mlx--dt.metallib # clean tree (unchanged key) mlx--w-dt.metallib # dirty tree ``` A clean tree hashes to the empty-input digest and keeps its **existing** key, so current caches stay valid and committed builds are byte-for-byte unaffected. A dirty tree now rebuilds once per distinct source state and prints which content hash it keyed on. ## Before / After ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Before A1[edit mlx kernel source] --> B1["key = HEAD sha + target"] B1 --> C1{cache hit?} C1 -- yes --> D1[reuse PRE-EDIT metallib] D1 --> E1[host/kernel ABI mismatch] E1 --> F1[GPU hang at 0% CPU
or silently wrong benchmark] end subgraph After A2[edit mlx kernel source] --> B2["key = HEAD sha + tracked diff
+ untracked contents + target"] B2 --> C2{cache hit?} C2 -- no, tree changed --> D2[rebuild metallib from actual sources] C2 -- yes, identical tree --> E2[reuse correct metallib] D2 --> F2[host and kernel agree] E2 --> F2 end ``` ## Verification Reproduced the stale hit (`Using cached metallib for d5a240408508`, hash `2e535253…`) against patched sources, applied the fix, and confirmed the same tree now rebuilds to a different metallib (`6b3099c9…`). Clean-tree runs still resolve to the original cache entry. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled.

items.title: fix: let a broken capture/stats/audit sink be heard (#131)
items.body:
Closes #131.

## The bug

`Interceptor._warn_sink` documents its own contract as: the **first** failure of each sink kind is written *unconditionally* — a sink failing on every call (full disk, bad path) would else go silent forever without `--debug`.

In the `run_proxy` / `run_multi_proxy` paths it could never fire. The callbacks handed to the `Interceptor` already caught their own exceptions behind a `--debug` gate (`_build_capture_and_audit` in `proxy.py`, `build_stats_writer` in `stats.py`), so the surrounding `try/except → _warn_sink` never saw one. The unconditional first-failure warning was dead code.

Observable: point `--capture-dir` at a regular file, or `--stats-log` at a directory, and you get a completely normal-looking run — every tool call answered, exit 0 — with **zero payloads captured, no ledger written, and nothing on stderr**. A later `terse measure --corpus` then reports a codec percentage over whatever subset happened to land.

## The fix

One owner for sink-failure *reporting*. The callbacks now own I/O and nothing else and let failures propagate; the `Interceptor` — the single caller, and the one already holding the per-sink bookkeeping (`_sink_warned`) — swallows and announces.

The fail-open contract is untouched. All five sink call sites are already inside a guard, so a sink failure still cannot change what the client receives; it is now merely *audible*:

```
[terse-proxy] gh.api.items: capture skipped: [Errno 17] File exists: '/tmp/not-a-dir' (further occurrences silenced unless --debug)
```

`Interceptor` gains `log_prefix` (default `[terse-proxy]`) so a multiproxy peer's failure is still attributed to `[terse-multiproxy]` — the only thing the builders' `log_prefix` argument bought. That bookkeeping is per-peer there, so the guard is once per **(peer, kind)**; the tests and docs pin that explicitly rather than overpromising one line per run. The attribution is the point, and the flood guard still holds within each peer.

### Rejected alternatives

- **Return a failure signal from the callbacks** — a second error channel alongside exceptions, for no gain; the callbacks have exactly two consumers.
- **Leave the swallow, warn inside the builders** — duplicates the once-per-kind bookkeeping in three places and splits it from the `_sink_warned` state that already lives on the `Interceptor`.
- **Do nothing, document it** — the failure mode is a silently wrong benchmark, which is the exact thing `_warn_sink` was written for.

## Tests

Five new cases, each pinning "a broken sink warns once on stderr **without** `--debug`, and the client's traffic is unaffected":

- `test_run_proxy_broken_capture_warns_once_without_debug` — two failing calls, exactly one warning, and the results still decode losslessly
- `test_run_proxy_broken_audit_log_warns_without_debug`
- `test_run_proxy_broken_stats_log_warns_without_debug` — the on-by-default sink, so the one most likely to go unnoticed
- `test_broken_stats_sink_warns_once_per_peer_under_the_multiproxy_prefix` — two peers × two calls → exactly two warnings, each peer-attributed
- `test_build_stats_writer_propagates_failures` — replaces the old swallow test

All of them **fail on the pre-fix code** (0 warnings observed against the stashed `src/`).

`uv run ruff check .` clean, `uv run mypy` clean, `uv run pytest -q` → **676 passed**.

Docs updated: CHANGELOG (Unreleased/Fixed), TECHNICAL.md (the `stats.py` contract paragraph), USAGE.md (a troubleshooting note with the real stderr line, captured from an actual run rather than composed).

items.title: fix(final-pass): a window minted behind the coverage frontier can still be re-transcribed (playhead-jzj0)
items.body:
`FinalPassRetranscriptionRunner.eligibleWindows` required `endTime > watermark`. Once the first batch's post-roll job drove `finalPassCoverageEndTime` to EOF, **every window ending inside the episode became permanently ineligible** — so any candidate or user mark arriving later could never get final-pass audio. The watermark measures **forward progress** and was being read as **completion**; candidate arrival is not monotonic.

## The witness

On `DE0784D8`, chunks overlapping **2838.18–2953.68** are **fast 122 / final 0**. That span is exactly Dan's two `userCorrection` windows at confidence 1.0. The asset holds **329 final chunks overall**, spanning 0→5522.65 — so this is not "final pass never ran", it is **final pass ran everywhere except where the user said it mattered**. And `finalPassCoverageEndTime = 5522.6776` against `episodeDurationSec = 5522.6514`: the frontier sits **past EOF**, observed.

Across two independent DBs, **11 of 14 job-less windows are excluded by the watermark alone**. A natural experiment in `db-evening2`: a window arriving 573 s after the frontier settled but *past* it got a job; four higher-confidence windows arriving 3.7 h later *behind* it got none.

## The fix

One deleted `guard` plus one moved-and-gated read. The per-window record it stood in for — `findFinalPassJob` + `guard job.status != .complete` — is monotone, durable and order-independent, i.e. genuinely what the frontier was pretending to be. A first attempt using a span-membership set was **backed out**: filtering before the grouping loop skips that loop's alias recording and would have silently narrowed `playhead-hygc.1.5`'s audit contract.

## R1's HIGH — which this bead's own fix would have unmasked

**A window whose span moves under a stable AdWindow id was re-decoded and re-ASR'd on every admitted sweep, for ever.** A job's identity is its canonical span, but its id is `fpj-<asset>-<adWindowId>` — and an AdWindow id is *stable across a span change by design*. After a shift the span lookup missed, `insertOrIgnoreFinalPassJob` was silently ignored on the PK, and the drain ran off a local struct claiming `.queued` for a row that was `complete`: `markFinalPassJobRunning` no-op'd, a full decode + ASR ran, `markFinalPassJobComplete` changed nothing, and the revalidation re-fired. The watermark had been suppressing the whole path.

Fixed by span-qualifying a clashing jobId **and** reading back the row the insert actually left behind.

## Review — three rounds, and each corrected the last

- **R1** found and fixed the HIGH; re-verified the 122/0 headline exactly.
- **R2** mutated R1's read-back and **the mutant survived, 91/91 green** — step 2 was entirely unpinned, step 1 alone satisfied every existing assertion. Added the missing rail. It also corrected R1's rationale: id determinism is true but is *not* what carries convergence (the insert stamps the span key from the row's own bounds, so the next sweep finds it by span regardless of id), and an unplug never enters `retryCount` at all (gate trips route to `deferred`, which does not bump).
- **R3** mutated R1's step 1 — also killed — and independently confirmed the two "comment-only" files really are comment-only, by stripping comments from both revisions and diffing.

`vbp8` (no retry cap) was upheld twice with reasoning: a cap can only be a count, a count cannot distinguish transient from deterministic failure, and the row it retires first is the one tried most — which on this bead's evidence is disproportionately a user mark at confidence 1.0. That is the permanent-exclusion class this bead exists to close.

## Gate — RED, verified, and not this branch

```
Executed 964 tests, with 30 tests skipped and 0 failures (0 unexpected)
gate-baseline: RED (47 known / 29 NEW)
GATE_EXIT=65
```

- **No wedge**; terminal verdict. **Zero XCTest failures.** **Zero Swift Testing failures under 97 s** — the fastest is 113.2 s.
- **Zero failures name a file this branch touched.** Both of the branch's own suites passed, including all seven jzj0/R1/R2 tests.
- **82 of 83 baseline members ran.** The one `DID NOT RUN` is labelled "renamed, deleted or newly skipped" and **that label is wrong**: `benchmark gate: 3 episodes finish under the orchestration budget` started at log line 11261, the host restarted at 49481, and it never completed. It still exists at `Phase3ShadowReplayHarnessTests.swift:184`. A restart artifact; this branch touches no integration test.
- Host restarted once, so the Swift Testing summary covers only the relaunch; real totals are 10,964 passed / 58 failed.
- **29 NEW and 2 deterministic entries passing — an improvement on the previous run's 32 and 17.** A baseline refresh is owed **on main**.

## Filed, not fixed

`8ykk` (complete rows retained for spans no AdWindow holds), `b0en` (the 0.5 floor was calibrated against a column that meant something else pre-`ar60`), `l8w1` (`coversWindow` is a per-CHUNK containment test that essentially never fires), `vbp8`.
