items.title: Pre-gate _auto_migrate so touching a database never writes to it
items.body:
`get_connection()` runs `_auto_migrate` on the first connection per DB path, and two of its statements were issued unconditionally: the Real-Assets label `UPDATE` (whenever an `asset_classes` table exists) and the pseudonym `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` (whenever the column exists). The `UPDATE` demands write access at statement start **even when it matches zero rows**, which is why merely reading a read-only `demo.db`/`tracker.db` produced `attempt to write a readonly database`. Both now sit behind condition checks that are themselves pure reads.

This is the last automatic write-on-touch channel in the codebase, after PR #165 (no DB access at import) and PR #168 (tracked data files are read-only committed inputs).

## What this is actually for

Not the test-failure count — this:

```
── the six PR #165 call-time lookups, personal book, READ-ONLY connection ──
  _intl_core_label()            -> 'International Developed'
  _sleeve_label(developed_exus) -> 'International Developed Sleeve'
  em_disclosure()               -> ok (425 chars)
  sleeve_names()                -> ['US Large Core', 'US Large Quality', … 9 sleeves]
  get_portfolio_account_id()    -> 1
```

PR #165 made those six lookups call-time so a warm process would pick up a sleeve rename instead of freezing the pre-split name. The side effect was that every factor regression, every methodology note, and the PDF factor section began routing through `get_connection()` — and therefore through a write-attempt. **All six now resolve against a genuinely read-only database.** A read-only diagnostic of the personal book — the recurring workflow this repo runs to make `git status --porcelain` a trustworthy gate — no longer perturbs what it is measuring.

## The heal is kept, not retired

Retirement was on the table and had a real case: no live DB matches the condition (0 rows in both `demo.db` and `tracker.db`), and the only match on disk sits in a gitignored backup that `get_db_path()` can never return. Measurement killed it. Of the three legacy labels, only two fail loud downstream:

```
'VNQ+DBC'               -> ValueError (weights sum to 2.0)
'VNQ+DJP'               -> ValueError (weights sum to 2.0)
'VNQ (50%) + DBC (50%)' -> PARSES CLEANLY as [('VNQ',0.5),('DBC',0.5)]
```

An unhealed book on the third label feeds a 50/50 Real-Assets benchmark into attribution and the quarterly PDF with **no error anywhere**, and nothing else in the stack catches it. `data/tracker.db.bak` is in exactly that state on its sub-class row, and its realistic reachability path is precisely the dangerous one: restoring it as the live book, which is when a silently wrong benchmark is least likely to be noticed. Retirement was a *means* to write-freedom; the gate delivers that without discarding a heal for a silent-wrong case.

The predicate lives in one shared `_REAL_ASSETS_LEGACY_WHERE` constant used verbatim by both the gate and the `UPDATE`. The silent-disable failure mode here is gate-drifts-from-guarded, and sharing the string makes that structurally impossible rather than merely test-caught.

## Coverage, stated honestly

**m3's write-freedom is proven.** **m4's gate is a correctness improvement resting on code review.** SQLite elides `CREATE … IF NOT EXISTS` for an already-existing object below the authorizer as well as below the write lock — measured: with the index present the authorizer sees nothing; with it dropped it sees `CREATE_INDEX`. So no runtime observation point can see whether that call is gated. What *is* tested for m4 is the other direction — that gating it did not disable it. No source-text grep was written to paper over this; a grep would have looked like coverage and verified nothing.

## Proof (`tests/test_db_no_write_on_touch.py`, 9 legs, none CI-deselected)

Four legs prove no write is demanded or issued against a DB needing no migration — `file:…?mode=ro` URIs (SQLite-enforced, so it cannot pass vacuously as a root-run `chmod 0o444` would) plus a `sqlite3` authorizer that names the offender. Five legs prove the migrations still heal: the label parametrized over **all three** legacy values including the silent one, the parent row and unrelated sleeves left alone, an already-correct label untouched, and the pseudonym index still created when genuinely absent.

Copies use `copyfile` + explicit `chmod`, never `shutil.copy` — see #173.

## Verification

- Proof **red first** on the parent (4 failed / 5 passed, all four at `src/db.py:236`, authorizer naming `['UPDATE asset_classes.benchmark_ticker']`) → **green 9/9** after → **red again** in a worktree of `83cdf61`.
- Guards-up full suite: **6 failed / 1551 passed** vs the controlled baseline of 15 failed / 1533 passed at `83cdf61`. **All nine write-on-touch artifacts cured**, including the two that run in a subprocess (`test_app_py_importable_offline`, `test_macro_page_importable_offline`) via `app.py`'s `initialize_db()`. Zero new failures; all 9 added tests pass. The remaining 6 are the 3 `shutil.copy` fixture artifacts (#173, deliberately out of scope — they survive every option considered here) and 3 pre-existing failures unrelated to this channel.
- Guards-down: **3 failed / 1554 passed** vs 3 failed / 1545 passed — identical three failures, the +9 being the new tests. Zero change.
- Headless personal-mode render against a scratch copy, writable and read-only, as above.

Related: #173 (fixture defect that misattributes evidence during exactly these diagnostics), #174 (whether the #165 import guard should extend to `pages/`).

items.title: [strategy] Automatically Tune Behavior
items.body:
## Summary

- Adds an adaptive policy to `commonware_parallel::Rayon` so `Strategy` operations can choose serial or parallel execution per callsite.
- Keys decisions by `#[track_caller]` location, operation kind, input length bucket, and Rayon parallelism.
- Samples both parallel and serial execution, tracks EWMA timings, and periodically re-samples to adapt to workload/platform changes.
- Removes the QMDB floor-candidate manual chunking at the callsite; candidate classification now maps over the actual candidate stream and lets `Strategy` choose execution.

## Performance

QMDB merkleize benchmarks were rerun with isolated Cargo target directories to avoid reusing the wrong benchmark binary from the shared build cache.

- PR head: `f7f7449e00a8c686c1d667a19d78418fb7bbef1d`
- Base head: `23b224eedb64d8ee1be8d47f42b404eebadaf088`
- PR target dir: `/tmp/qmdb-target-automatic-rayon`
- Base target dir: `/tmp/qmdb-target-main`
- Command template:

```bash
RUSTFLAGS='--cfg full_bench' \
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<isolated-target> \
CRITERION_HOME=<isolated-criterion-home> \
cargo bench -q -p commonware-storage --features test-traits --bench qmdb -- '<filter>'
```

Lower is better:

| QMDB merkleize filter | Base | This PR | Improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `current::unordered::fixed::mmb chunk=32 keys=10000 ch=false sync=false` | 919.97 us | 498.83 us | 45.8% |
| `current::unordered::fixed::mmb chunk=32 keys=100000 ch=false sync=false` | 4.6462 ms | 4.0655 ms | 12.5% |
| `current::unordered::fixed::mmb chunk=256 keys=100000 ch=false sync=false` | 4.3651 ms | 3.9045 ms | 10.6% |
| `current::ordered::fixed::mmb chunk=32 keys=10000 ch=false sync=false` | 1.0034 ms | 575.62 us | 42.6% |
| `any::unordered::fixed::mmb keys=10000 ch=false sync=false` | 731.34 us | 413.09 us | 43.5% |

I also prototyped moving coarse chunking into `parallel` for vector-map helpers. It did not materially improve the simplified QMDB path, so that broader behavior change was left out.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p commonware-parallel`
- `cargo check -p commonware-storage --all-targets --features test-traits`
- `cargo fmt --all` (emits the repo's existing stable-rustfmt warnings for nightly-only rustfmt options)

items.title: Make 'make benchmarks' work again
items.body:
Follow-up to #141, independent of it. `make benchmarks` has been broken for a while; this gets it building and running again. Tested on macOS with Apple clang 21 and GCC 15; `make` and `make test` are unaffected.

### `oneoff/convert_benchmark.c` no longer compiles

0d9c323 ("make SDR transfer size a variable", Aug 2022) replaced `MODES_MAG_BUF_SAMPLES` with the runtime `Modes.sdr_buf_samples` but didn't update the benchmark:

```
oneoff/convert_benchmark.c:70:22: error: use of undeclared identifier 'MODES_MAG_BUF_SAMPLES'
```

The benchmark has no SDR, so I defined the constant locally from today's startup default (`sdr_buf_size` 128 kiB, 2 bytes per sample = 64k samples). The pre-2022 value was 256 kiB / 2; I went with the current default as the more meaningful number, but say the word if you'd rather keep the historic one.

It also needs `Modes` and `setExit()`, which `util.o` references and which live in `readsb.c` — that can't be linked in here since it has its own `main()` — so they're defined locally in the benchmark.

### The link rule is stale

Even with the object compiling, the link fails with a page of undefined symbols: the rule still lists `convert.o util.o` and `-lm`, but `util.o` has since picked up `threadpool.o`, zlib and zstd. Switched to `$(LDFLAGS) $(LIBS)` and added `threadpool.o` and `$(COMPAT)`.

### The target runs the wrong path

`benchmarks:` ran `./convert_benchmark`, but the binary is built as `oneoff/convert_benchmark`, so the target would have failed even with everything else fixed. `make clean` had the matching problem — it removed `./convert_benchmark` and left `oneoff/*.o` and the actual binary behind.

### `htole16` is missing on macOS

The Apple branch of `compat/compat.h` defines `le16toh`/`le32toh` but not the reverse, so the benchmark's `htole16()` calls fail to build. Added `htole16`/`htole32` next to them. Only the benchmark uses them today.

For reference, the result on an M-series Mac:

```
Benchmarking: UC8, no DC     2876.92M samples/second
Benchmarking: UC8, DC         343.98M samples/second
Benchmarking: SC16, no DC    1014.00M samples/second
Benchmarking: SC16, DC        351.00M samples/second
Benchmarking: SC16Q11, no DC 1027.05M samples/second
Benchmarking: SC16Q11, DC     351.36M samples/second
```

items.title: feat(funds): Phase-2 — server-side risk-metrics engine (volatility, maxDrawdown, 52w)
items.body:
## Phase 2 — the metrics that beat the competitor's broken `maxDrawdown=0`

Computes **correct** fund risk metrics deterministically from our own `nav_history` — no scraping, no external feed, no wrong-benchmark assumptions. A competitor shows a drawdown number but computes it wrong (0 on funds that clearly fell); ours is right and comes from data we already refresh daily.

### Backend
- **`data_pipeline/fund_metrics.py`** — PURE math (stdlib only, unit-testable): returns (1m/3m/6m/ytd/1y/3y/5y), **annualized volatility scaled by the series' ACTUAL sampling frequency** (not a blind √252 — EG fund NAVs are weekly), **`max_drawdown`** (running-peak; `0.0` when monotonic-up, `None` when <2 pts), 52w high/low.
- **`tests/test_fund_metrics.py`** — 13 unit tests with hand-verified answers (drawdown −25%, weekly-vol 72.23%, bad-point rejection, window/ytd edges). Runs under pytest **or** standalone.
- **`scripts/compute_fund_metrics.py`** — reads `nav_history`, **self-migrates** the companion table `fund_risk_metrics` (`CREATE IF NOT EXISTS`), idempotent `ON CONFLICT` upsert. Uses `connect_resilient` + **read-only preflight** + **never-false-green** (exit 2 if < `--min-updated`).
- **`app/services/scheduler.py`** — `tier4d_fund_metrics`, 08:30 & 19:30 Cairo Sun-Thu (30 min after the NAV refresh). Isolated subprocess; a failure never crashes the API.

### Frontend (isolated side-table pattern — can never break the core fund payload)
- **`/api/v1/funds/[id]`** + **`getFund`**: `fund_risk_metrics` read in try/catch (same fail-safe pattern as `peers`/`actions`). Advanced metrics always from the table; returns/52w **fill gaps only**, never override `funds_view`.
- **`Funds/[id]/page.tsx`**: new **"Risk & Volatility"** section (Max drawdown, annualized Volatility). Renders only when data exists → no empty/broken UI if the job hasn't run yet.
- **Sharpe / alpha / beta intentionally omitted** until a real EGX benchmark + EGP risk-free rate are wired (a wrong Sharpe is worse than a blank one).

### Safety / architecture
- **No `funds_view` / `mutual_funds` change.** New table is self-migrating and side-joined — a schema issue there is isolated.
- Read-only-incident safe; idempotent; never-false-green.

### Verification
- **13/13 unit tests pass** (drawdown, frequency-annualized volatility, returns, 52w, bad-data handling).
- `py_compile` on all Python; SQL placeholder alignment checked (15 params); `tsc --noEmit` clean on all 3 frontend files.

### ⚠️ One access-gated follow-up
A GitHub Actions workflow (`funds-metrics.yml`) is the preferred scheduler but **could not be pushed — this token lacks `workflow` scope**. Scheduling is therefore wired into the backend APScheduler instead (pushable, runs on the same Hetzner box). If you prefer the Actions path, add `funds-metrics.yml` with a workflow-scoped token (content provided by the assistant).

items.body:
## What

Builds the **foundation of the Silent Wrong-Effect benchmark** (design doc `.private/benchmark_design_2026_07_20.md`, top-3 item #1) — the clean, documented **contract** the multi-baseline runner adapter (#2) and the task pack (#3) will depend on. Generalizes the two existing artifacts named in the design doc:

- `benchmark/fault_model/` — the MockMed `GET /api/db` DB-state oracle + `classify()` (5/7 transactional fault classes silently mishandled by screen-only). **The reusable core.**
- `benchmark/silent_wrong_action/` — the proto-SWER rate: 55.6% wrong-by-screen → 0.0% wrong-by-effect over 90 runs. **The measurement template.**

## New package `openadapt_flow.benchmark.effectbench` (linted + type-checked)

- **`schema.py`** — episode data contract (pydantic): `TaskSpec`, `OracleSpec`, `EpisodeRecord`, `AgentReport`, `ModelCall`, and the `OutcomeLabel` taxonomy — **success / safe-halt / over-halt / silent-wrong-effect / false-abort / wrong-action**. `SWER = |silent_wrong_effect| / N` by construction.
- **`oracle.py`** — the substrate-agnostic effect-oracle harness generalizing the fault_model DB-state oracle: `classify_outcome` (the taxonomy as one total function of oracle × self-report × action-availability), `score_episode` (runner orchestrator), `RecordSnapshotOracle` (in-memory pluggable core), `combine_true_states` (compound `record_written` + `field_equals` contracts). The four concrete substrates (SQL / REST / FHIR / file) are the runtime `EffectVerifier`s, re-exported. Every oracle reads **pre/post system-of-record state, never the screen or the agent's report** (non-gameable).
- **`metrics.py`** — `summarize` → `BenchmarkSummary`: SWER (+ wrong-write / phantom split), over-halt, task success, **success–effect gap**, cost/latency, `pass^k`, with Wilson + bootstrap CIs, **always decomposed by category × substrate** (no aggregate-only reporting).
- **`README.md`** — the stable contract for the downstream agents, with verbatim signatures.

`benchmark/effectbench/reference_fault_model.py` re-expresses the existing fault_model episodes through the new schema + harness and reproduces the known result, pinned by `tests/test_effectbench.py`:

items.title: Delete TURN_MODE: measure the three turn modes, keep only smart-turn
items.body:
Stacked on #26 (`perf-latency`). Measures #26's three `TURN_MODE` options, then deletes the two that lose. Net **−197 lines** in `server.py`.

## Answer to "can E4B or 12B judge turns better than E2B?"

12B is genuinely better than E2B/E4B — and still not close to the 8M-parameter classifier it would replace.

| Mode | Model | Accuracy | Interrupt rate | p50 decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **smart** (smart-turn-v3.2) | — | **0.960** | **0.070** | **19ms** |
| marker | E2B | 0.500 | 1.000 | 664ms |
| marker | E4B | 0.500 | 1.000 | 1179ms |
| marker | 12B | 0.660 | 0.640 | 3578ms |
| two_phase | E2B | 0.560 | 0.000 | 619ms |
| two_phase | E4B | 0.500 | 1.000 | 1123ms |
| two_phase | 12B | 0.660 | 0.680 | 3766ms |

`smart` on 200 real English clips, LLM rows on 50. *Interrupt rate* = unfinished turns wrongly judged finished, i.e. cutting the user off.

E2B and E4B are degenerate — they answer one label to everything (E2B two_phase answers WAIT to almost everything, which is why its 0.560 comes with 0.120 finished-recall: it would simply never reply). **E4B buys nothing over E2B at double the latency.** 12B actually discriminates, but trails smart-turn by 30 points, interrupts on two thirds of unfinished turns, and takes 3.5s to decide.

**Verdict: ship the classifier alone.** `TURN_MODE` is gone.

## Why the LLM modes fail — the audio path, not the prompt

#26 tried five prompt variants. The cause is narrower:

- Asked to **transcribe** the same clips, E4B is accurate — the audio arrives intact.
- Judging that **transcript as text**: 14/20. Judging the **audio**: 10/20.

The turn signal survives into the transcript and is destroyed in the FINISHED/WAIT decision when the input is audio. No prompt rewrite recovers that; only an ASR-first architecture would, at the cost of a full transcription pass to land below an 8M-parameter model. llama.cpp also still marks Gemma audio input experimental.

## What the removal takes with it

The marker regex and kinds, two extra system prompts, the two_phase decision request, `run_turn`'s `expect_marker` and its incomplete path, and StreamParser's entire marker branch — the parser is now just response-then-transcript. Completeness is decided before the LLM is called, so any turn reaching `run_turn` is complete by construction.

`benchmarks/turnbench.py` keeps both prompts, so the comparison re-runs against the next Gemma without digging them out of git history.

## Correction

The first commit's numbers were wrong. `_marker_verdict` compared against `"incomplete"` while `MARKER_KINDS` maps WAIT to `"incomplete_short"`, so every LLM verdict parsed as complete — which is what produced the tidy "all three sit at 0.500". Fixed in 2b67767; the table above is the corrected run. The conclusion did not change, but "12B is at chance" was wrong.

## Benchmark used

[`pipecat-ai/smart-turn-data-v3.2-test`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/pipecat-ai/smart-turn-data-v3.2-test) — 31,527 clips, 23 languages, `endpoint_bool` ground truth. Fetched via the HF datasets-server REST API and cached as 16kHz WAVs, so no new dependency.

Restricted to `synthetic=false`: TTS clips read as finished whatever the words are — the same effect that makes #26's `thinking_suppressed` check fail by construction. Note **all 971 Indonesian clips are synthetic**, so this set cannot validate the Bule-AI multilingual case; `--synthetic` opts in with that caveat.

**This is smart-turn's own test split**, so 0.960 is in-domain and optimistic. [LiveKit's eot-bench](https://github.com/livekit/eot-bench) (Apache-2.0, 14 real languages including Indonesian) scores smart-turn v3.2 at 35.2% false cutoffs against a 300ms budget — the independent cross-check worth running.

## Threshold: left at pipecat's default

`turn_detector.py:56` uses `probability > 0.5`, which matches pipecat's own default ([`local_smart_turn_v3.py:174`](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/blob/main/src/pipecat/audio/turn/smart_turn/local_smart_turn_v3.py)). Unchanged. For the record, 0.6 scored better on this data (0.975 accuracy, interrupts 0.070 → 0.030), but that is a 200-clip in-domain tune against an upstream default, so it stays as a note.

Worth a follow-up: pipecat pairs the classifier with `stop_secs=3`, a silence fallback that force-completes a turn regardless of the classifier. Parlor has no equivalent — it nudges instead.

## Verification

`benchmarks/bench.py` against the rebuilt server: every correctness check passes except `thinking_suppressed` (documented in #26 as failing by construction). Latencies unchanged — `audio_short` first audio 0.573s, `audio_long` 0.688s.

items.title: study2: correct the public record, freeze the eval inputs, preregister study 2
items.body:
Brings `main` up to date with the study-2 branch. The immediate reason is that the public README currently contradicts the project's own evidence.

## What `main` says today, and why it is wrong

> BFCL benchmark numbers are not yet available. Formal evaluation ... is scheduled for Week 7

> **DPO v2: designed, optional scope.**

Both are stale. BFCL v4 `simple_python` was run and committed; DPO v2 was run and closed as a documented negative result. A reader checking the repo against the shipped claims would conclude the 92.25% headline is unsupported.

## What this changes

**The public record.** SFT scored **369/400 = 92.25%** on the 400-item pinned set. DPO v2 is closed as a second negative result — held-out tool-use came in below SFT at every evaluated checkpoint (364/363/359 against 369), with no contrast significant after Holm correction. The earlier `n=399` text was a newline-counting error; the score itself was always 92.25%.

bootstrap guard (#313) was reporting `composer.json is not present yet` and skipping every
toolchain job. This lands the build system that flips that guard.

Item **1.6** ships in the same PR because it is the same file: "pin composer.json identity"
*is* the content of the `composer.json` that 1.1 creates. Writing 1.1 without it would mean
committing a deliberately wrong identity and correcting it one PR later.

## Change

- **`composer.json`** — package `egl/utils`; PSR-4 autoloading `D4np\Utils\` →

  import, *Alternatives #5*); requires PHP `>=8.1` with `ext-pdo` and `ext-fileinfo`, plus the
  interface-only `psr/container` and `psr/log` — which **RFC-0001 R-3** explicitly excepted
  from the spec's literal "zero-dependency" wording, because a package implementing PSR-11 and
  PSR-3 necessarily requires their interface packages.
- **`composer.lock`** — committed, per the language profile (`composer.lock committed`).
  Resolved: `psr/container` 2.0.2, `psr/log` 3.0.2.
- **Component-group skeleton** under `src/main/php/d4np/utils/` — `Dto`, `Container`,
  `Database`, `Security`, `Http`, `Errors`, `Support`: RFC-0001's C4 grouping made real.
  **Structure only** — each group's behavior belongs to its own milestone (M2–M6), so nothing
  here anticipates later work.
- **Docs in the same PR** (§7): `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]` entry, `ROADMAP.md` checkboxes
  1.1 / 1.6 flipped, and the session journal
  [`2026-08-03-pipeline-bootstrap-and-build-system.md`](docs/journal/2026/08/2026-08-03-pipeline-bootstrap-and-build-system.md)
  with the *Latest checkpoint* pointer.
- **New roadmap item 1.8** (§10: out-of-scope findings are filed, not dropped) — the
  `version_file` path in `tools/consistency_lint.py` `CONFIG` is **doubled**
  (`src/main/php/d4np/utils/src/main/php/d4np/utils/Version.php`): the scaffold manifest passed
  a full path where the template already prepends `SRC_MAIN`. Harmless while the file is absent
  (the check falls back to the README badge), but it would silently disarm `version-lockstep`
  the moment item 1.5 lands — the lesson **L-0008** failure class, a gate that stays green
  while asserting nothing. Filed to be fixed *with* 1.5, proving the gate can fail.

## ⚠️ CI goes red with this PR — by maintainer decision

Landing `composer.json` flips the bootstrap guard, so the toolchain jobs start running **for
real**. Verified on this PR's run — each failure identified by its actual failing step, not
assumed:

| Job | Failing step | Cleared by |
|---|---|---|
| `build` ×3 (8.1/8.2/8.3), `lowest-deps` | `vendor/bin/phpunit` | item **1.2** |
| `quality` | `php-cs-fixer` | item **1.3** |
| `hygiene` | `composer normalize` | item **1.3** (`ergebnis/composer-normalize`) |
| `benchmark` | `vendor/bin/phpbench` | **item 1.9** (filed) — *not* 1.2/1.3 |

**Green:** `consistency / lint`, `bootstrap`, and — thanks to the step-level config guard added
during scaffold — `quality / deptrac layer rules` and `quality / infection mutation score`,
which self-skip until their configs land.

**Correction (§12.4).** When proposing the scope split the agent predicted the red set as
"build, quality, hygiene, lowest-deps" and claimed 1.2 + 1.3 would restore a fully green
matrix. Both were wrong: `benchmark` also runs (the `bench` capability is on) and fails on a
dev dependency no M1 item introduces. Filed as **item 1.9**, which also records a latent defect
in that job — its `php-version` expression reads `matrix.toolchain` in a job that declares no
matrix, so the ternary silently falls through to `'8.3'`.

The agent proposed bundling M1 into a single green PR and **dissented** from the split on the

items.title: fix(bench): a reused reference worktree could benchmark the wrong commit
items.body:
Both `materialise()` implementations decided a cached reference worktree was reusable by testing that `.cache/<gate>-<sha>/src/index.ts` exists. Existence proves a worktree is there, not which commit it holds.

They now verify the contents against the requested sha and rebuild on mismatch.

## What was wrong

- The sha appears in the directory *name*. Nothing checked it against the directory *contents*.
- A worktree left by an interrupted run, or checked out elsewhere, was reused silently.
- The gate then benchmarked a different commit from the one it named in its own output, with no warning.

## What it checks now

Both `bench/grammar-perf-guard.ts` and the shared `bench/ab-harness.ts`:

- `git rev-parse HEAD` in the cache directory must equal `git rev-parse <sha>` in the root.
- `git status --porcelain -- src` must be empty. Being *at* the sha is not enough: a tracked modification under `src/` means the benchmark imports code the sha does not name. `copyPaths` are overwritten from the working tree by design and live outside `src/`, so scoping to `src/` catches the real case without rebuilding every run.
- An unverifiable cache is treated as stale, and the reason is printed rather than swallowed. A rebuild is cheap; a confidently wrong number is not.
- The verification git calls are bounded at 10s, so a hung git cannot hang the gate.

## Why it matters beyond the fix

This retroactively weakens every number these gates have produced. Any past result whose reference side came from a reused `.cache/` directory may have been measured against the wrong commit, and there is no way to tell after the fact which ones were — the output recorded the sha it *intended*, not the sha it *used*. The defect erased its own blast radius.

Combined with the interleaving artifact from #79, these gates had two independent ways of producing a confident wrong number, one of which was invisible in their output. Both are now fixed. Neither fix recovers the historical record.

<details>
<summary>Notes</summary>

Found while reviewing the cross-process script, not by a failing gate — no test reported it, because a test that could report it would have to know the right answer independently.

Also documents the AST-only differential blind spot alongside the harness one in `docs/design/perf-harness-interleaving.md`, and corrects a CST characterization in that file: the observed delta was duplicate removal, not token loss.

Review findings: Greptile's P1 (a dirty worktree passes a HEAD-only check) is fixed by the `git status --porcelain -- src` check. CodeRabbit's timeout finding is fixed by `VERIFY_TIMEOUT_MS`. Its further suggestion to *rethrow* on timeout was deliberately not taken — a transient local git hiccup should rebuild, not hard-fail the gate; the `console.warn` addresses the actual complaint, which was silent swallowing.

Touches only `bench/` and `docs/`, so no published surface changes and no version bump is required.

</details>

items.title: [#2282] docs(mission): Phase 0 forensic audit — the gap is evidence, not features [19c13ec]
items.body:
The Mission 10/10 directive's first instruction is to **audit before writing any code**, and that instruction earns its place: this is the third large external directive reviewed against this codebase in one session, and the first two both described systems that **already existed**. One of them, followed literally, would have re-broken a shipped fix that had already bricked the app once (`launchAutoHide`).

## The finding

**This platform is strong on implementation and weak on proof.**

318 AgentV3 modules · 289 with co-located tests (91%) · **14,070 tests passing**. Nearly every capability the directive asks for exists, is wired, and is tested. What almost none of it has is **field evidence** — measured behaviour on real builds.

Applied honestly, the directive's own §3 (real-world verification required) and §39 (no score without evidence) cap most dimensions at **7–8** — not because the code is weak, but because **we have not measured it**. The scorecard that would measure it shipped hours ago (#2277) and currently holds **zero builds**.

So the highest-value action is not to build anything: it is to run real builds through the measurement we now have. Every `UNKNOWN` becomes knowable within days of traffic, at no engineering cost.

## Four gaps are genuine rather than unmeasured

1. **Multi-service execution** — the graph describes topology (#2278); nothing starts a second process
2. **Autonomous E2E journey derivation** — scaffolding exists, journeys do not
3. **Adversarial security tests** — strong controls exist; nothing attacks them
4. **Benchmarks** — none

## ⚠️ The cost warning the directive never states

It says *"operate autonomously, do not wait after every phase"*. Right for code, **wrong for benchmarks**: each benchmark build is a **real build spending real money**.

Measured on this platform today: **₹150–₹567 per build**.

| Benchmark | Builds | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| §9 500-edit survival | 500 | **₹75,000 – ₹2,80,000** |
| §36 Golden suite | 10+ | ₹1,500 – ₹6,000 |
| §11/§12 full matrix | thousands | **lakhs** |

That is the admin's provider spend, not compute time. **Benchmark phases stop for budget approval (§44); everything else proceeds autonomously.**

A cheaper and less gameable substitute already exists: the builder scorecard computes edit survival from **real user projects**. §53 forbids nursing a curated benchmark — and a hand-picked 500-edit app is exactly the thing that gets nursed.

## No score here is 10/10

And none will be until there is evidence behind it. Phases 1–6 (all free) begin next.

items.title: fix: correct tier-2/3 CER (<DR> editor-token contamination) + v0.1.1 corrections
items.body:
## The public benchmark ships wrong numbers

`benchmark-v0.1.0` reports tier-2 CER **0.0172** and tier-3 **0.0234**. Both are wrong.

| figure | v0.1.0 (withdrawn) | corrected |
|---|---|---|
| tier-2 CER, B vs consensus | 0.0172 [0.0105, 0.0248] | **0.0031 [0.0006, 0.0062]** |
| tier-3 CER, B vs consensus | 0.0234 [0.0166, 0.0309] | **0.0119 [0.0085, 0.0156]** |
| adjudication, tier-2 edits | 165 | **33** |
| adjudication, tier-3 edits | 280 | **148** |

## Cause

`<DR>`, the annotator-tool token for a double *rafe*, was scored as four literal ASCII characters in the tier-2/3 CER path. `iaa/cer.py` asserted editor tokens were "already stripped during `split_chunks`" — they were not. `split_chunks` strips only `PASSTHRU_TAGS`, and `<DR>` is deliberately excluded so tier-4 extraction can emit a `double_rafe` record from it. Nothing removed it afterwards.

The three sides carry unequal counts (A 25, B 56, consensus 27), so every excess token scored as four spurious edits.

Self-contradictory as well as wrong: `strip.py` already excludes U+05BF (*rafe*) from tier 2 precisely "so it is not double-counted across tiers". The single *rafe* was stripped; the double *rafe*, in ASCII, was not.

## Direction

**Conservative.** The bug made the two annotators look *less* consistent than they are. No conclusion reverses.

## Not affected

Verified field-by-field over regenerated result JSONs — **262 tier-4 and stratification fields compared, zero changed**: tier-1 CER 0.0029; tier-4 F1 exact 0.9187; Krippendorff α 0.7470; BL-05 *rafe* baseline F1 0.6210; every corpus count. Tier 1 is immune because its projection keeps only Hebrew consonants, space and *maqaf*.

## Also in this PR

- **`personnel_note` removed** from four public fixtures — it named a collaborator in full alongside an internal personnel correction and referenced a private-repo file. It remains in the immutable `v0.1.0` tag.
- **David Zev Moster added** to `CITATION.cff`, README citation, `LICENSE.md` attribution and `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS.md`. He produced half the reported agreement and was named only in the changelog and data files, while his projection ships under attribution-required terms.
- **Two false statements removed from this repo's own documentation.** `generate_iaa_report.py` claimed in two places that the headline CER was "NOT recomputable without the gitignored UXLC 2.5 cache." Tiers 1–3 recompute from the three committed projections alone. **Two independent external reviewers repeated that claim in their audits, having taken it from this docstring rather than testing it.**
- The shipped `_note` described the metric as code-point Levenshtein on NFC; it is cluster-aligned code-point CER on NFD, macro-averaged over verses.

## Structural fix

`masoretic_eval.iaa.cer.tier_view()` is now the single definition of a chunk's scoring view. The same sequence had been inlined in **three** places — `cer.py`, `scripts/generate_iaa_report.py`, and the release test meant to guard reproducibility — and the latter two would have silently missed the new strip.

Regression test `tests/iaa/test_editor_token_cer_isolation.py` asserts tier CER is invariant to editor tokens at every tier, and that tier-4 extraction still consumes `<DR>`.

## Gates

- `pytest` — 360 passed, 8 skipped
- `generate_iaa_report.py --check` — ok
- `verify_gt_hash.py --check` — ok
- `audit_release.py --all --release-tier` — **PASS**

## Provenance

Found while verifying three independent external reviews of `benchmark-v0.1.0`. The tier-3 half was flagged by the Codex reviewer; the larger tier-2 half and the adjudication-count contamination were found during verification of that finding.

  ────────────────────              ───────────────────────
  include/EASTL           ──►       Choosing a Container: A Decision Guide
  allocator.h             ──►       Anatomy of an Allocation
  fixed_*.h               ──►       When You Cannot Touch the Heap
  intrusive_*.h           ──►       When the Container Should Not Own the Memory
  internal/config.h       ──►       204 Switches: Configuring EASTL for a Shipping Build

  doc/Gotchas.md          ──►       Ways to Get This Wrong
  test/ + benchmark/      ──►       (compressed into one page, by instruction)
```

24 pages, 8 `repo_notes`, all flat (no `parent`) so the manual reads as an ordered narrative.

| Problem | Measurement | Instruction |
|---|---|---|

Introduces **Ω-SKILLGEN-T∞**, an OAK-safe recursive **Agent Skill civilization foundry** for ChatGPT/Codex: compiler, evaluator, generator-of-generators, population laboratory, evidence-memory loop, lineage system, Generator Discovery bridge, and standalone installable packaging pipeline.

- `SkillSpec -> SKILL.md + evals + provenance` compiler
- static lint and activation-boundary checks
- TrustGate for approval bypass, credentials, destructive/exfiltration language, and epistemic overclaim

The foundry evolves **populations**, not just prompt variants.

- independent objectives can track behavioral pass rate, activation precision/recall, OAK score, novelty, reuse, risk, cost, and complexity

items.title: fix: reconcile speakers across independently-diarized parts of long recordings
items.body:
## Summary

- **Bug fixed:** Recordings longer than 30 minutes are auto-segmented into 30-minute parts, each diarized independently. The final merge (`mergeSegmentTranscriptions`) silently dropped **all** speaker data — `segment.speaker`, `word.speaker`, `speakerEmbeddings`, and `speakerCount` — from the merged `TranscriptionResult`. Long meetings had no speaker attribution, no voice-library matching, and wrong benchmark counts.
- **New pure helper `SegmentSpeakerReconciler`:** Reconciles each part's local speaker IDs into one global speaker space via greedy one-to-one voiceprint cosine matching (threshold 0.5). Parts missing embeddings yield distinct new globals — never a mislabel.
- **Wired into `RecordingManager`:** `SegmentTranscriptionPiece` gains `speakerEmbeddings`; `mergeSegmentTranscriptions` remaps `segment.speaker` and `word.speaker` through the reconciler, and `transcribeSegmentedAudio` forwards `speakerCount` and `speakerEmbeddings` on the final result.

## What reviewers should know

- `SegmentSpeakerReconciler` lives in the app target (`Sources/dBrief/Services/`) — it reuses `VoiceMatch.cosineSimilarity`, which is also app-target only. No wire/protocol/helper-process changes.
- The existing 3-arg `SegmentTranscriptionPiece` call site in `mergeSegmentTranscriptionsAppliesOffsets` is preserved unchanged via an explicit init with a default `speakerEmbeddings: nil` parameter (stored-property `= nil` isn't synthesized into Swift 6 memberwise inits).
- The reconciler does **not** match against the persisted voice library — `VoiceIdentityResolver` owns that downstream once `speakerEmbeddings` is populated.
- Graceful degradation: a part whose embedding extraction failed yields new distinct globals rather than risk a wrong label, consistent with the project's "neutral Speaker N beats a confident wrong name" stance.
- 416/416 tests green.

## Test plan

- [x] `swift test --filter SegmentSpeakerReconcilerTests` — 6 unit tests covering same-speaker merge, different-speaker separation, 3-part/2-person, missing embeddings, no-diarization passthrough, determinism
- [x] `swift test --filter WhisperPipelineTests` — 12 tests, including new `mergeForwardsSpeakerData` (asserts speakers unified, words remapped, offset preserved, `speakerCount == 1`, embeddings forwarded) and existing offset test still green
- [x] `swift test` — 416/416 all suites

items.title: fix(evidence): attribute each real-time margin to its percentile (DAR-209)
items.body:
Part of DAR-207. Closes DAR-209.

`/evidence/benchmarks` read:

> A deployed end-to-end controller measures ≈52 µs p50 / ≈94 µs p99 — the figure to cite for whole-controller latency. It clears the 10 ms real-time budget by roughly **190×**.

Two latencies, one margin, no statement of which it divided. It was the p50 one — and under a real-time budget the **tail** is what decides whether the loop holds, so the single figure published was the one that mattered least, and it is the one a reviewer recomputes first. The review did exactly that.

Nothing was false: 190× at p50 and ~100× at p99 describe the same controller. That is why this is DAR-117's **disclosure** axis rather than the truth one — and why the sibling surface made it worse instead of catching it. `evidence_realtime_not_covered` said "roughly two orders of magnitude", a ~p99 claim also unattributed, so a reader meeting the two in either order concluded the other was wrong.

## What changed

Every real-time margin is now **computed** in `$lib/evidence.ts` by one `realtimeMargin()` from the control budget and a percentile-named latency constant, so no margin on the site is hand-typed and none can drift from its input. Both surfaces render the same p99 constant and name the percentile. `REALTIME_MULTIPLE` is derived too — byte-identical to the `'13,000×'` string it replaces (verified) — because leaving one margin hand-typed beside two that are not is how a fourth gets hand-typed.

The controller section also gained a dated line, a methodology field and an environment field. Not decoration: the kernel section had all three and the controller had none, and that asymmetry is what let a noisy shared-container figure read as a tight constant.

## Reading the artifact changed two things the ticket got wrong

**The published p99 was wrong.** `benchmarks/results/quadrotor-cascade--run1.txt` records `p99= 98.654 us` in its data table, while its own headline *comment* says `p99 ~= 94 us`. The site had the comment's figure — a tail no artifact contains, **understated**, which flatters every margin derived from it. Now ≈99 µs, with the run-to-run spread disclosed.

**The ticket's proposed copy reproduced the defect one level down.** It asked for "≈106× at p99", which is three significant figures over an input whose source of record says to treat as *"tens of microseconds on this class of x86 box, not a tight constant"* — so it moves with the noise. Rounded down to two, 94 µs and 99 µs **both publish 100×**: the correction does not move the headline at all, which is the coarseness doing its job. Rounding is fixed **downward** for the same reason — one significant figure would publish 192.3 as 200×, larger than anything measured, in our own favour.

## Guards

| file | pins |
| -- | -- |
| `evidence.spec.ts` (new) | the reader's own recomputation as an inequality; rounds down never up; the separator; and each published percentile against the top of the spread the environment copy states — the assertion that would have caught the 94 µs |
| `evidence-disclosure.spec.ts` | every published margin names the percentile it came from, with the retired sentence as a negative control |
| the e2e | which constant reaches which placeholder — invisible to every unit spec |

The attribution matcher is deliberately **not** a proximity window. Both margins live in one sentence, so a window wide enough for the connective in "at p50 it clears by roughly 190×" (22 chars) also reaches 28 chars across to the *wrong* percentile — a swapped pair would read as attributed. It resolves the nearest percentile inside the same sentence and returns the token, so one assertion covers unattributed (null) and mis-attributed (the other token).

## Mutations

Every one caught, each by exactly one file:

| mutation | result |
| -- | -- |
| percentile labels stripped from the copy | disclosure spec, 1 failure |
| margin arguments swapped at the call site | **unit 27/27 green**, evidence e2e 1 failure (`190× at p50`) |
| `{margin}` placeholder removed from the message | `pnpm check` **0 errors**, disclosure spec 1 failure |
| round to nearest instead of down | evidence spec, 2 failures |
| three significant figures | evidence spec, 2 failures |
| one latency constant for both percentiles | unit green, e2e 1 failure (`≈99 µs p99`) |
| p99 lowered back to 94 | evidence spec, 1 failure (spread guard) |

That third row is DAR-117's Paraglide finding with a polarity attached, measured here: *adding* a placeholder makes every call site a `pnpm check` error, so wiring a figure in cannot be half-done — but taking one back *out* leaves `Inputs = {}`, which accepts any object literal, so the call site keeps compiling while the page silently loses its attribution.

## Verification

lint 0 · `pnpm check` 0 errors · **1390 unit** · **113 e2e**

(One full unit run reported 3 collection errors — `ContactDialog`, `/news`, `/research`, none touched here — under loadavg 31.6 on 12 CPUs; all three pass on re-run and the DAR-90 report records `failedTests: 0`.)

items.title: Pine: fix single-symbol idle-cash sizing + add Timed-vs-SIP comparison
items.body:
Two related Pine improvements, both isolated to `pine/`.

## 1. `dip_mafia_strategy.pine` — kill the single-symbol idle-cash drag (`8d1c6a6`)
On one symbol, ₹10k fixed-cash tranches against ₹1,000,000 `initial_capital` left ~99% of the account in idle cash, which crushed the strategy's % return and Sharpe versus Buy & Hold (the RANEHOLDIN confusion).
- New **"Position sizing"** input, default **Percent of equity (25%)**, capped at available cash (`equity − holding value`, less a hair for the 0.05% commission) so a buy is never rejected for insufficient funds and the account actually gets deployed. Fixed-cash mode preserves the old behaviour.
- Added **Buy & Hold (from 1st buy)** and **Strategy − B&H (pp)** rows to the metrics table for an apples-to-apples on-chart read.

## 2. `dip_mafia_sip_vs_timed.pine` — new Timed HODL vs SIP indicator (`9eba235`)
A `strategy()` can't receive periodic cash, so it can't model "salary arrives monthly and gets deployed into dips" — and TradingView's day-1 Buy & Hold is the wrong benchmark when cash arrives over time. This new **indicator** hand-rolls the accounting:
- adds a flat **monthly contribution** (₹/mo input) to a cash pool after the 200-bar warmup;
- **Timed HODL**: deploy into dip signals; deploy idle cash after N bars (the single-symbol reduction of `backtest.py`'s V4 fallback);
- **SIP**: deploy the month's cash immediately;
- plots both equity curves + Invested, with a table (mult / return / **Timed − SIP** in ₹ and pp), green when Timed wins.
- Benchmark is **SIP, not Buy & Hold**. On-chart analog of `simulate_timed_hodl` vs `simulate_sip`.

## Honest caveats
- Single-symbol: **no** cross-stock fallback or 15%-per-stock cap (portfolio-level; those stay in `backtest.py` / the dashboard). A name that rarely dips can still trail SIP — that's real, not a bug.
- Shows multiple + total return, not money-weighted XIRR (an IRR solver is fragile in Pine).

items.title: docs: ADR-0016 — Shrap is a multi-asset, continuously-operating firm
items.body:
**Merging this = accepting that Shrap trades US equities, MES futures and spot
crypto, operating continuously — and that the NautilusTrader migration moves
from deferred to scheduled.**

Your ruling: *"I want Shrap to trade 24/7 stocks, MES, and crypto."*

> **Corrected after review.** The first draft claimed FINRA's pattern-day-trader
> rule blocked intraday trading at $10k and built the whole justification on it.
> Mike caught it: **the PDT rule was eliminated effective 2026-06-04** (SEC
> approval 2026-04-14, SR-FINRA-2025-017; FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10). The
> decision is unchanged; the sequence and the urgency both changed. The ADR
> carries a Corrections section rather than editing the error away.

## The regulatory position

No $25,000 minimum. No pattern-day-trader designation. No day-trade counting.
**Margin requires $2,000 minimum equity.** Intraday equity trading at $10k has
been available for seven weeks.

**What replaced PDT matters more to us than PDT did** — a continuous,
position-based regime instead of a trade counter:

- **25% maintenance margin** on long margin-eligible equity, held *throughout
  the trading day* — an effective intraday leverage ceiling near 4x.
- An **intraday margin deficit** calculation: the largest shortfall between
  required margin and available equity when margin-reducing trades occur.
- Deficits unmet within five business days, **plus a pattern of
  non-compliance → a 90-day freeze on new positions.**

That last one is specific to an autonomous firm: an agent doesn't get tired, and
a repeated breach takes the whole firm offline for a quarter.

## The target, recorded honestly

| | Multiple | CAGR | Per day |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kotegawa, ~$13.6k → ~$153M / 8y | 11,250× | **221%/yr** | **0.46%** |
| Same run framed as 6y → $180M | 12,000× | **379%/yr** | **0.62%** |
| 1%/day (raised, then set aside) | — | 1,130%/yr | 1.00% |
| 35%/yr | — | 35%/yr | 0.12% |

The most-cited retail run in history compounded at **about half a percent a
day**. Noted alongside: survivorship (he's known *because* he's the tail), the
correction that comparing a $10k account to fund Sharpe was my wrong benchmark
(funds are capacity-constrained; $10k isn't), and Mike's point that **his path
was methodical, not frantic**.

## Frequency is a capability, not a quota

Mike, 2026-07-29: *"it doesn't have to make trades every day — we want smart
trades. It can do it all day if it thinks the day is going to be good for it."*

Recorded as a binding design constraint: no agent gets a trade-count target,
"no signal today" is never an error state, and turnover stays a **cost** in the
Evaluator rather than a virtue. This ADR buys the *ability* to trade intraday,
not an obligation to.

The honest tension is stated too: selectivity shrinks sample size, and
`DEFAULT_MIN_TRADES` exists because small samples lie. It resolves through
**breadth, not a lower gate** — already measured: 89 trades on one ticker,
28,139 across fifty. A selective strategy over many instruments clears the gate;
over one instrument it does not, and should not.

## What 24/7 actually means

| Asset | Real hours | Margin regime |
|---|---|---|
| Spot crypto | genuinely 24/7 | own rules |
| MES futures | Sun 18:00 → Fri 17:00 ET, daily 60-min halt (~23/5) | CFTC/exchange |
| US equities | 09:30–16:00 ET regular; 04:00–20:00 extended | FINRA intraday margin |

The firm can be *awake* 24/7. Only crypto trades all of it.

## Sequence — reordered by the correction

1. **Intraday equities.** Cheapest by far: reuses the broker, the 50-name
   universe, Tier 3, the strategies, the Evaluator. Needs two things — intraday
   bars, and a Runner that fires more than once per session. No new calendar, no
   ADR-0003 gate if bars are polled rather than streamed.
2. **Spot crypto** — the genuine 24/7 piece, and what actually forces per-venue
   calendars and a session concept with no open or close.
3. **MES**, behind the NautilusTrader validation card *and* Risk Officer bounds.
4. **Extended/overnight equities**, once broker capability is verified.

## This still trips the ADR-0003 gate

ADR-0003 names "real-time market data feeds" and "multi-venue routing
(IBKR/MES)" explicitly, and says *"IBKR/MES work cannot start before that
gate."* Merging accepts that the NautilusTrader validation becomes scheduled
work.

## The risk I want stated, not buried

**Margin is reachable by a $10k account today**, and the firm has **no drawdown
limit, no leverage bound, no per-strategy loss limit, and no model of the
intraday margin deficit.** The PDT correction makes this a *live* exposure, not
a futures prerequisite — which is why Risk Officer limits moved to card 2.7,
ahead of everything else in this track.

## Unverified — flagged rather than assumed

Broker crypto availability in paper · extended/overnight equity access · MES
margin requirements · whether our paper account reflects the post-2026-06-04
margin regime · whether the account is margin or cash.

Docs only. Independent of #119.

Sources: [FINRA Notice 26-10](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/notices/26-10) · [FINRA intraday margin](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/intraday-margin-requirements) · [SR-FINRA-2025-017](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/finra/2026/34-105226.pdf)

items.body:
Replaces JSON on the wire with Protobuf, generated for Go and C# from one schema, with a migration path that needs no coordinated deploy.

Motivated by [`BENCHMARK.md`](backend/docs/BENCHMARK.md) (PR #39): snapshot build + JSON was ~80% of tick cost, and ADR-7's own `< 50 KB/s per client` threshold broke at ~41 players.

## Results — measured, and smaller than the estimate

Three arms at matched player counts, **one loadtest binary held constant**, so only the server varies. Full data in [`BENCHMARK.md` Part II](backend/docs/BENCHMARK.md).

| | baseline (develop) | new, JSON | new, Protobuf |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Tick ceiling (p99 < 66.67ms) | **150** | **200** | **300** |
| KB/s per client @ 150 | 183.8 | 183.4 | **80.7** |
| Bandwidth ceiling (< 50 KB/s) | ~41 | ~41 | **~93** |

Bandwidth saving is a flat **~55%** from 50 to 250 players. Tick ceiling doubled, 150 → 300.

**Three honest caveats, all documented rather than buried:**

1. **~55%, not the ~70% the estimate implied.** Protobuf removes field names, punctuation and float formatting; it cannot remove identifiers. A 15-char entity ID is ~15 of a packed entity's ~40 bytes.
2. **Only about half the tick win is the encoding.** The middle arm exists precisely to expose this: removing a stray `JsonDocument.Parse` round-trip moved the ceiling 150 → 200 on its own; Protobuf moved it 200 → 300.
3. **ADR-7's bandwidth threshold still fails**, at ~93 players instead of ~41. Bandwidth remains the binding constraint and the absolute gap to the tick ceiling *widened* (109 → 207 players). **A dense-crowd capacity plan should use ~93, not 300.** The next lever is reducing what is sent, not how it is encoded.

Baseline reproduced Part I within noise (61.1 vs 61 KB/s @ 50; tick p99 49.77ms vs 49.77ms @ 150), which is what makes the comparison trustworthy.

## Design

**One schema, two generators.** `backend/shared/proto/wire.proto` is the source of truth; `generate.sh` emits Go and C#. Both outputs are committed so no runner needs protoc, and a new `proto-generated` CI job regenerates and fails on any diff to stop them drifting.

**No parallel hand-written definitions.** The C# hand-written mirrors of the Go structs are **deleted** — the generated types are now the game server's only message classes. Legacy JSON is produced by a hand-written `Utf8JsonWriter`/`Utf8JsonReader` codec over those same generated types, so there is still exactly one definition of each message. (Protobuf's `JsonFormatter` was rejected: camelCase output plus descriptor reflection, incompatible with both this wire format and AOT.)

**Migration by content sniffing, not negotiation.** A JSON body always starts with `{` (0x7B); a Protobuf `Envelope` always starts with `0x08` (tag for field 1, `type`, which proto3 never elides since `type >= 1`). One byte identifies the encoding — no version field, no handshake, no round trip. Encoding is latched **per connection** and a server always replies in the encoding it was addressed in.

That means the gateway, game servers and Unity client upgrade **in any order**, with no flag day and no window where a mismatched pair breaks. It also makes the benchmark single-variable: `-encoding json|proto` A/B-tests one unchanged binary. Rationale in [ADR-9](backend/docs/ARCHITECTURE-DECISIONS.md).

Framing (`[4-byte BE length][body]`) is untouched, so `shared/transport` and the TCP/KCP layer needed no changes.

## NativeAOT

Hard requirement, checked first rather than last. `dotnet publish -c Release` with `PublishAot`: **zero trim/AOT warnings**, 17.4M binary. `Google.Protobuf` uses generated, not reflection-based, serializers.

## Verification

- Go: 199 shared / 139 gateway / 76 smoketest / 98 loadtest — all pass, `go vet` clean
- C#: 369 tests pass
- **Integration (the one that matters): `TestDotnetInterop_FullFlow` now runs the whole Go-gateway ↔ C#-server handshake in *both* encodings** — the only test that can prove the two independently generated implementations agree. Plus `TestDotnetInterop_MixedEncodingsOnOneServer`, a JSON client and a Protobuf client on the same running server, asserting each gets replies in its own encoding.

## Bugs found and fixed on the way

- **Game server dropped the handshake's encoding.** The join handshake runs on a throwaway `Connection`; the session one was built fresh afterwards, so every reply fell back to JSON. Caught by the mixed-encoding test.
- **`Connection.Encoding` had a visibility race** (written by the read loop, read by the tick loop) — now `volatile`. Found in review, not by a test.
- **loadtest's snapshot loop hardcoded `json.Unmarshal`**, so under proto every snapshot silently failed to parse and was skipped — it surfaced as `recv%=0`, i.e. "the server sent nothing", which would have produced a confidently wrong benchmark.

## Follow-ups noted for later (not in this PR)

1. **Bandwidth is still the binding constraint** — ~93 players against a 300-player tick ceiling, and the absolute gap *widened*. ~40% of a packed `EntitySnapshot` is now `id`/`type` string data that no encoding can compress. Interning entity IDs and making `entity.type` an enum are the remaining levers on the wire itself; after that it is sending less (AOI radius, distance-tiered update rates). Sized in `shared/docs/DESIGN.md`. **This likely matters more than this PR did** — this bought headroom, that addresses what actually breaks the threshold.

2. **The join handshake runs on a throwaway `Connection`.** The handshake reads on a temporary connection and the session one is built fresh over the same socket afterwards, so *any* per-connection state observed during the handshake is silently dropped unless handed over explicitly. This PR hit it with the wire encoding; negotiated compression, a client-declared version, a per-connection cipher or an observed MTU would each be lost the same way — and silently, because the fresh connection's defaults are always valid, just wrong. Written up in `gameserver-dotnet/docs/DESIGN.md` so the next person adding per-connection state knows.

## Review order

The commits are a deliberate sequence — schema → Go → C# → callers → tests → benchmark — and read best in order. `backend/shared/proto/gen/**` and `GameServer/Net/Generated/**` are generated; skip them.

Deliberately out of scope, with reasons in `shared/docs/DESIGN.md`: interning entity IDs and making `entity.type` an enum. Both would shrink the hottest message further but change what the field *means*, whereas this is a pure re-encoding.

items.title: feat: measure and reclaim a store's substrate bytes
items.body:
A quiet store never triggers SlateDB's size-tiered scheduler, so months of churn stay readable-through forever — a production catalog held 3.4 GB while serving one snapshot, with a read-only attach taking 642 s, and nothing shipped could say what those bytes were or reclaim them. `moraine_store_census('lake')` now reports, per subspace, physical bytes and SST/sorted-run counts from the manifest, plus store-wide totals by object kind (log, manifest, SST, other) from one listing — the gap between `store_sst_bytes` and `store_total_bytes` is what says whether a merge is even the right lever, since an unpinned read attach replays the write-ahead log before it materializes anything and no merge touches those bytes. It serves a `READ_ONLY` attach, and `live := true` adds a scan separating live keys from dead weight. `moraine_compact_store('lake')` merges a subspace's sorted runs into one, on demand or as step 8 of the maintenance pass; moraine picks no sources and no destination, and the plan SlateDB makes for a whole tree destines its bottom run, so tombstones and superseded versions drop rather than move.

RFC 0021 is revised rather than superseded — its "forcing SlateDB compaction" rejection is answered reason by reason — and the same edit corrects prose PR #77 left stale about maintenance batches writing `sys/head`.

Three defects were found by testing and measuring rather than by reading, and each is fixed here. Submitting a full-tree plan while the background scheduler merges the same runs trips an `assert!` inside slatedb's executor. Worse, guarding against that by skipping made an on-demand merge reclaim *nothing* in its most common case — opening a writer starts a compactor that proposes immediately, so a merge asked for straight after an attach found every tree busy; a busy tree is now adopted and waited on instead. And the census originally counted SST bytes only, so a store whose weight is its log would have read as nearly empty and pointed an operator at the wrong lever.

`BENCHMARK.md` gains two measurements: cold attach cost against physical bytes (which sharpened the claim — a read point-reads `sys/head` and the head `snapshot` record as well as scanning `current`), and attach cost under injected per-GET latency, which prices the merge in the IO-bound regime the incident sat in (14.5 GETs → 12.3, 147 ms → 125 ms at 10 ms/GET). Full local gate green including `cargo xtask e2e` (88 ducklake_load tests).

items.title: protocol(doc-gate): preflight checks the committed RANGE — --staged was vacuous
items.body:
Self-reported protocol violation from PR #80, and the gate change that prevents it recurring.

## What went wrong

PR #80 (Vulkan) landed **eight commits** that touched `src/` and `tests/` without updating `docs/STATUS.md` and `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` **in the same commit**, so `documentation-checkpoint` failed for that push range on `main`:

`9579f94e`, `ba5ea0cf`, `196ea46f`, `e32c5ed3`, `3bfa1f12`, `34a3efe6`, `2c86f79e`, `f4738bb8`

Each deferred its doc update into a following `record(...)` commit.

## Why it passed locally — the part actually worth fixing

`check-doc-checkpoint.py --staged` inspects the **staged** paths. It is therefore **vacuous when nothing is staged** — which is the normal state after `git commit`, and exactly when `agent-preflight.sh` runs it. The gate reported OK on every one of those commits while checking literally nothing.

CI is **diff-scoped** over the pushed range and checks each commit independently, so the failure only appeared on `main` — where, by that job's own design, a diff-scoped range is never re-covered by a later run.

## The fix

`agent-preflight.sh` now runs `--base origin/main --head HEAD` whenever the branch is ahead of main, reproducing CI's verdict locally in seconds.

That check sits **outside** the `--staged` block, deliberately. My first attempt nested it inside, which reproduces the identical hole one level up: `--staged` is precisely the flag you are *not* passing when the range goes unchecked. Caught by the gate catching my own commit, which is the best evidence it works.

Verified two ways:
- prints `ok doc-checkpoint range` on this branch;
- pointed at the #80 range (`075b9f21..0be5d457`) it raises **20 errors** naming every offending commit.

`workflow.md` carries the same instruction with the reason, so the next series doesn't rediscover it.

## What is *not* being done

**History is not being rewritten.** `main` had already moved (#86 landed on top) and other sessions branch from it, so force-pushing to regroup eight commits' files would cost more than the defect is worth.

**The substance was never wrong.** STATUS, BENCHMARKS and FEATURES on `main` all describe the shipped Vulkan state accurately, with the llvmpipe-only and no-speed-number caveats intact. What was violated is the per-**commit** granularity that keeps a bisect landing on a commit whose docs match its code, and stops a half-landed series from leaving the public surface describing something that doesn't exist.

Recorded in the state log rather than quietly left, since that range stays permanently gate-failed.

## Unrelated pre-existing red

`agent-record` was already failing on `main` at `4cfeee13`, before the #80 merge — `check-fusion-consistency` on `minimax_h3_video_vae_device`. Verified on `origin/main` itself. Not from this work, and not addressed here.

items.title: command3: test the benchmark suite directly and document what it proves
items.body:
## The gap

`modelBenchmarks.ts` had **no direct tests**. `benchmarkLedger.test.ts` reaches it only through aggregation, so a definition could lose its `successCriterion`, or `sampleBenchmarks` could start returning the whole suite, without anything failing.

Both are failures that surface as provider spend rather than a red build — the wrong place to find them.

## Tests added (17)

`backend/src/ai/modelBenchmarks.test.ts`, covering the parts that cost money when wrong:

- Every benchmark states how it is settled without asking a model (`objective`, `successCriterion`, `evidenceKind` all non-empty).
- Benchmark ids are unique — duplicates would silently merge two measurements into one ledger entry.
- Sampling is capped at 8 and never returns the whole suite; §21 forbids running it all on a user request.
- Heavy benchmarks are dropped first, so measurement cost stays below the cost of the work being measured.
- A narrow filter yields the heavy benchmark rather than silence — returning nothing would read as "unmeasurable" when it is only expensive.
- A language filter does not exclude `language: null` benchmarks, which would drop review, debugging and refactor coverage the moment a language was named.
- A failed result never records under the evidence kind a success would have produced (`tests_passed` → `tests_failed`, `patch_applied` → `patch_rejected`, `repair_succeeded` → `repair_failed`).
- An empty history summarises to `null`, not `0` — "never measured" and "0% pass rate" are different claims.
- Median latency is the middle, not the mean.

## Documentation

Three new documents, each covering ground no existing document did:

| Document | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `docs/model-evaluation-system.md` | The suite, the ledger seam, the eight maturity gates, and how measured evidence reaches `chooseCostAware` |
| `docs/learning-data-governance.md` | The five learning-data kinds, the eight capture conditions, and why fine-tuning consent is not implied by data-use permission |
| `docs/migration-and-rollback.md` | The three conditions a migration slice must meet, what has landed, what has not, and how each step is undone |

The evaluation doc states plainly that **no runner executes the suite against live providers**. The definitions, scoring shape, aggregation and routing consumption all exist and are tested; the component that spends provider budget to populate them does not. A suite that looks complete and has never run is the most misleading artifact in an evaluation system, so it is named rather than left to be discovered.

`docs/universal-agent-rollout.md` said:

> The *enabled* path is not yet wired: no real build routes through `planUniversalRun` to generate files, so setting `enabled` today changes only the routing decision.

That has been false since `pipeline.ts` began routing through `atomicGitHubCommit` (`pipeline.ts:1168`, `:1214`). A document asserting the opposite of current behaviour is worse than no document. items.title: test(conn): measure conn, and run the gates that never ran
items.body:
## Why

Neither `conn` benchmark measured `conn`, and two allocation gates were guarding
nothing. Both were invisible in a green run.

## What was wrong

**The benchmarks**, three independent ways:

1. The peer was `httptest` + `net/http2` over TLS **in the same process**, and
   `b.ReportAllocs()` counts every goroutine in the binary. An exact
   `-memprofilerate=1` profile put only **10.2** of the 34 allocs/op on
   conn+frame; the other **23.6** were the server, the TLS handshake, and
   `time.Time.Format` rendering the server's own `Date` header.
2. The loops never called `Close()`, so `streamPool` took no `Put` at all —
   `&Stream{}` fired 2001 times per 2000 requests, a **0% hit rate**.
3. They dropped `StreamEvent.Slab`/`DataSlab` instead of returning them. `conn`
   hands pooled buffers out and never reclaims them itself (only `client` does,
   in `Response.Reset`/`sr.Close`), so `headerSlabPool` missed twice per request.

**The gates.** A `//go:build !race` test escapes CI if its package is missing
from the gate step *or* its name misses the `-run` pattern. Both had happened:
`./conn/` was absent, and `TestCallOptions_AreStillApplied` /
`_EndToEndStillHonoured` matched no alternative — those being the correctness
half of the callopts gate, the tests that exist so the ceiling cannot pass on a
helper nothing calls. Verified before fixing: each printed `[no tests to run]`
and passed green.

## What changed

`conn/bench_peer_test.go` (new): an h2c peer on `frame.Framer` answering a
pre-encoded 204 — the shape `grpc/bench_test.go` and `client/bench_mock_test.go`
each already had. `benchDrain` closes the stream and returns both buffers.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `Roundtrip_Concurrent` | 34 allocs/op, 3794 B/op | **2**, ~100 B/op |
| `Roundtrip_Empty` | 36 allocs/op, 3790 B/op | **2**, 84 B/op |
| `streamPool` hit rate | 0% | **98%** |
| `!race` gates executing | 5 of 8 | **8 of 8** |

**No hot-path code changed** — the whole delta is the harness. Re-verified after
rebasing onto #572. TLS coverage stays in `groupcommit_bench_test.go`, which
counts writes and TLS records and so genuinely needs it.

## Answer to the question that started this

`grpc` can reach 0–1 allocs per unary RPC; streaming receive is already zero via
`RecvInto`. `conn` cannot join bench-gate's absolute zero, structurally — it
multiplexes N streams over one socket, so it has a reader goroutine, event
channels, and a shared-lifetime `*Stream`. The stale "deferred to B.2" note that
implied otherwise is replaced here. What `conn` *can* hold is a steady-state
per-request zero, now two allocations away: `string(f.Value)` in `authorityOf`
and `make([]HeaderField, n)` in `copyFieldsToSlab`.

Left out deliberately, both touching production code: `StreamEvent.Release()`
(−1 alloc, and it makes the bug class above unwritable) and a `Stream`-owned
`authorityBuf` (−1 alloc). The latter is **not** the one-line `authorityOf` →
`[]byte` it looks like — the value is stored for the stream's lifetime and read
by the PUSH_PROMISE authority check (RFC 9113 §8.4), so the copy is
load-bearing. A gate on the final number belongs with those.

items.title: perf(bench-ratchet): reduce -count samples by min, not mean
items.body:
Personal review PR (fork → fork). Benchmarking-infrastructure fix — not a VM change.

## Problem
`aggregateFromFile` averaged the N `-count` repetitions of each benchmark (`NSPerOp: nsSum / count`). Mean is the wrong reducer: benchmark noise is **one-directional** — GC pauses, CPU migration, a co-scheduled runner tenant, thermal throttling only ever make a run *slower*, never faster. One slow sample drags the mean up and manufactures a phantom regression.

That's precisely what we watched all session: the small (<20 ns) `BenchmarkGetOwn` variants flip-flopped **6 → 2 → 4** "regressions" across three otherwise-identical `perf-pr` runs, on code paths the PRs never touched.

## Fix
Reduce by **minimum** instead — the fastest of N repetitions is the least noise-contaminated estimate of true cost. Raw samples are still retained in `Samples` for provenance. alloc/bytes are deterministic per op, so min == mean for them.

## Evidence
Unit test (`main_test.go`, first test for the package) pins the min reduction: `{100, 140, 105}` → 100, not 115.

Local stability, `BenchmarkGetOwn/n=16/last`, count=6 × 3 captures:

| reducer | values across captures | spread |
|---|---|--:|
| mean-of-6 | 10.15 / 9.83 / 9.94 | 3.1% |
| **min-of-6** | 9.86 / 9.78 / 9.85 | **0.8%** |

~4× tighter even on a quiet local machine; the gap widens on a noisy CI runner where a single spike inflates only the mean.

## Caveats
- **`perf-pr` A/B benefits immediately and safely** — both halves are measured with the same reducer in one run, so this is a pure noise-floor reduction.
- **`perf-timeline`** snapshots on the `perf-data` branch were captured with mean, so the first snapshot after this lands steps down once (min < mean) — a one-commit discontinuity on the historical dashboard, not a real improvement.
- **Do not add the `perf` label to this PR** — it would compare base's mean-reducer against head's min-reducer (apples-to-oranges). Merge and it applies cleanly to subsequent PRs.

items.title: Add FLEXMEASURES_LP_SOLVER_OPTIONS to configure solver options
items.body:
## What

Solver options for the scheduling solver could previously only be set in code (a hardcoded HiGHS profile inside `device_scheduler`). This adds a `FLEXMEASURES_LP_SOLVER_OPTIONS` config dict, merged **over** that profile so operators can tune the solver without patching FlexMeasures:

```python
FLEXMEASURES_LP_SOLVER_OPTIONS = {"mip_rel_gap": "1e-4"}
```

## Validation (the important part)

When the solver is HiGHS, the options are **validated against the installed HiGHS build** before use. An unknown option name, an invalid value, or a feature the build lacks raises a clear `ValueError`.

This matters because Pyomo's `appsi_highs` interface applies options **without checking HiGHS' return status** — so a mistake is otherwise silently ignored. Concretely, `solver="hipo"` is unavailable in the pip-installed `highspy` (it needs a HiGHS built against BLAS + METIS), yet `appsi_highs` solves on as if nothing were wrong. Anyone benchmarking such an option would get a false negative. Validation turns that silent no-op into an explicit error.

Setting `threads`/`parallel` logs a warning: HiGHS initializes its thread scheduler once per process, so in a long-lived worker only the first solve honours them and later solves fail with `global scheduler has already been initialized`.

## Tests

`test_solver_options.py` covers: the shipped default profile stays acceptable, unknown names / invalid values / unavailable solvers raise, all rejected options are reported, and `threads` warns.

## Context

Found while investigating SeitaBV/ems#172 (benchmarking whether the HiGHS `hipo` solver helps the HEMS scheduler — it can't even be selected from the pip wheel, and `appsi_highs` was hiding that).

> **Prerequisite:** EBiM-Benchmark/benchmark#38 adds a Contributing section to benchmark's README. **Merge that first**, so the pointer this PR adds doesn't land on a README with no contributor tooling in it.

## Why

This file was written for the `benchmark` repo and later promoted to the org default — so it carried benchmark's assumptions to repos it was never about. Three sections were repo-specific dressed as universal:

| Section | Assumed | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| **Local setup** | every repo is a Python package (`pip install -e ".[dev]"` → `pre-commit install` → `pytest`) | Fails on **all four** public repos — including benchmark. See below. |
| **Code style** | every repo has pre-commit | true for `benchmark`; not for the others |
| **Reporting bugs** | Python + a simulator ("Include OS, Python version, sim version") | meaningless for a Node site, `submissions`, or `.github` |

**`pip install -e ".[dev]"` doesn't work in a single public repo — not even the one the guide was written for:**

- `benchmark` — `pyproject.toml` defines **no `[project]` and no `[build-system]`**, and there's no `setup.py`/`setup.cfg`. All 11 of its tables are `[tool.*]`; it's lint/type-check/test/spell configuration, nothing to install. benchmark's own README tree already calls it *"Repository-wide lint/type-check configuration"*.

items.title: Docs: Plan Binding What Arrived Instead of What Was Declared
items.body:
Design note only — no code. Follows the `local-` convention for proposed, not-yet-filed work.

`ParamBinder.bind` costs **1.28 μs**. #787 justified that against a 60 μs corpus median, where it is
2.1%. That is the wrong denominator.

`benchmarks/survey/752-baseline-main.csv`, 520 queries:

| | count | median engine time | binding share |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| whole corpus | 520 | 60.1 μs | 2.1% |
| exact-name (`!"..."`) | 95 (18%) | **7.3 μs** | **14.9%** |

The fastest are 2.7–3.4 μs, and 18% of the corpus runs under 10 μs. A fixed per-request cost lands
hardest where the engine is fastest, which is also the most common thing a user asks for.

## Where it goes

`search`, 10 parameters, 6 supplied:

| component | cost |
| --- | ---: |
| walk the 10-entry plan | 740 ns |
| collision check | 180 ns |
| `dict(zip(positional_names, args))` | 160 ns |
| dict copy + update | 90 ns |

`card` is the only one of 28 marked handlers that declares positional parameters, so for the other 27
the zip builds an empty dict and the intersection compares an empty key view — 340 ns to learn
nothing. And the loop visits all 10 declarations to fill 6 arrivals plus 4 defaults that never change.

## Proposed

Skip positional handling when `args` is empty, and iterate `supplied.items()` against a precomputed
defaults dict instead of walking the plan. Measured with full semantics preserved:

```
current                1.32 μs
restructured           0.65 μs   (2.03x)
```

## Why the doc rather than the patch

`bind` is small but every branch is load-bearing, and the change moves the loop from "declared
parameters" to "supplied names" — exactly where an omission hides. The doc enumerates eleven
invariants a rewrite has to hold, flags the two with no test today, and names one the change
*introduces*: copying a precomputed defaults dict is a shallow copy, so a mutable default would be
shared across requests. No handler has one now, and that should be asserted rather than assumed.

Three alternatives are recorded as rejected with the measurement that rejected them, including an
optimistic fast path with a careful-slow-path fallback — structurally sound, but 0.64 μs against
0.63 μs, because Python 3.11+ has zero-cost exceptions and skipping the `converter is None` guard
costs an extra dict lookup.

The open question is whether exact-name really dominates production traffic or is an artifact of the
corpus's shape. Access logs would settle it.

items.title: fix(claims): restate the CogniGate latency claim as its own published target
items.body:
Clears the Public Record Auditor's first blocked claim. Both pages published `~8ms p50 / ~20ms p95` as measured fact, and it reconciled with nothing.

## The obvious fix was wrong twice over

**Trap 1 — the nearest real number was the wrong row.** `vorion/docs/benchmarks/phase6-performance.md` measures `p50 12ms / p95 28ms`, which reads like a clean substitute. But look at the table:

| Endpoint | p50 | p95 |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /stats` | **12** | **28** |
| `POST /role-gates/evaluate` | 18 | 42 |
| `POST /ceiling/check` | 15 | 35 |

`12/28` is `GET /stats` — a dashboard read, and the *fastest* endpoint in the file. The policy-decision endpoint measures **18/42**. Using 12/28 would have put the fastest read endpoint on a résumé as a policy-decision latency.

**Trap 2 — the file benchmarks the wrong system.** Those are **Vorion Phase 6 Trust Engine** endpoints. The claim is about **CogniGate**, which has no measured latency artifact anywhere — the `p50` in `cognigate/tests/test_monte_carlo.py` is a probability variable (`analytical_failure_prob`), not a latency. Citing that file would have traded one mis-attribution for another that merely *looked* sourced.

## The honest resolution

Restate as **CogniGate's own published design budget** — `~38ms median / <120ms p99 decision target` — worded as a target, matching `cognigate.dev` verbatim.

In `claims.json` the claim moves from `unverified` to `attested` against that published budget: sourced, dated, and subject to the 180-day expiry. The full reasoning is recorded in the claim's `note` and in `research/CLAIMS.md` so nobody re-walks it.

Tooltips updated too — they explained p50/p95, which no longer applies. They now say plainly that this is a design target, not a measured benchmark.

## Result

```
Public record audit — 2026-07-26
  ✓ cognigate-latency — attested
  … 19 more
  · 0 blocked, 0 need review, 20 clean
```

Auditor exits 0 (was 19 clean / 1 blocked) and correctly writes no report, since there is nothing to escalate. `check:syntax` (89 checks) and `selftest:all` both pass.

## The lesson the gate now encodes

**A number is not sourced merely because a number exists somewhere.** It has to be the same measurement, of the same system. `no-unsourced-metric` catches the missing source — only a human reading the source catches the wrong one. Which is exactly why every correction routes to a human merge.
